#5783. 300 Glaciers Have Disappeared from the American West Since the Mid‑20th Century — the Survivors Have a Few Things in Common

From an airplane, most of the glaciers of the Rocky Mountain West look like small patches of white nestled into rugged landscape where the topography folds. The white is the snow cover, and lower down you can see the gray-blue bare ice.

In the middle of the 20th century, over 1,450 glaciers could be found in the contiguous U.S. Together, they covered 217 square miles (562 square kilometers) in six western states. Today, a comprehensive review my colleagues and I just published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences shows their total area has shrunk by 35% and they are still shrinking, perhaps faster.

A little more than 300 glaciers have disappeared, way more than I had anticipated.

Those that survive reflect just how vulnerable mountain glaciers have become as global temperatures rise. Where glaciers once covered large expanses of the western mountains thousands of years ago, most of the remaining glaciers in the Rockies and Sierra Nevada are small and found in topographically protected places.

When people think of glaciers, they often picture huge ice streams with icebergs calving off the front, like you’ll find in Alaska or Greenland. In the Lower 48 states, with the exception of a few large glaciers in Washington, they’re much smaller.

We found that the average glacier area is about one-tenth of a square mile (about a quarter of a square kilometer) in size. The area of the largest glacier, found on Washington’s Mount Rainier, is about 4.3 square miles (11.24 square kilometers).

I was surprised to find that glaciers in the Rocky Mountains – those in Colorado, Montana and Wyoming and in the Sierra Nevada of California – subsist because of their unique position on the landscape, which somewhat insulates them from the otherwise less-favorable regional climate.

The surviving Rocky Mountain glaciers inhabit shaded niches less exposed to direct sunshine and gain additional snow from avalanches. If these glaciers were exposed to more sun and less snow accumulation, they likely wouldn’t exit at all.

We found the fastest-thinning glaciers are in the Beartooth-Absaroka Mountains of the Rockies in southern Montana, which are losing about 1.5 feet (about half a meter) of ice thickness per year.

It’s a different story in Washington, where the glaciers on Mount Rainier and Mount Baker are much larger, have cooler summers and get a lot more snowfall. Although they too are shrinking, they do so at a much slower rate, about half a foot of ice thickness per year. The glacier area on Mount Rainier alone is greater than the total sum in all the other states.

In Washington, generally speaking, the higher you go, the less glacier loss you find. That makes sense; it’s cooler at higher elevations. But in the Rocky Mountain region there is no similar trend, suggesting the survivors are niche glaciers that depend on local topographic benefits.

In a study a few years ago, colleagues and I modeled the glaciers on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula and found most would disappear by 2070 under current climate trends. That indicates that glaciers elsewhere are probably not far behind.

The Olympics are vulnerable because they’re close to the Pacific Ocean at somewhat lower elevation. The other Washington glaciers, particularly on Mount Rainier and Mount Baker, will likely survive past 2100, but how much longer is an open question.

The principal importance of the glaciers is to provide water to high alpine ecosystems. The glaciers partially melt in late summer, providing cool water for cold-adapted fish and other stream life. They provide a water supply that’s otherwise absent in the dry late summer, after the seasonal snow disappears, when the region doesn’t get a lot of rain.

While the glaciers of the Rockies are primarily important for ecosystems at this point, those in Washington also contribute to hydropower production.

An important hazard is also associated with the glaciers on the steep-sided volcanoes of the Cascade Range, which stretches from California to Washington. The moraines formed by these glaciers are large, partly due to the highly erodible volcanic rock beneath the ice. Moving ice deposits eroded rocks, forming aprons at their lower ends. As the glaciers retreat, they leave the accumulated rocks behind as steep-sided moraines that are no longer buttressed by the ice.

High water flows from rain or glacier melt can undercut the moraines, triggering landslides and creating debris flows that go rocketing down the mountains. This happened in 2006 on Mount Hood and Mount Rainier and closed a number of highways. We’ll see that happen more often as the glaciers retreat.

The shrinking and eventual loss of all of these glaciers will affect ecosystems across the West, as well as waterways humans and wildlife rely on.

By Andrew Fountain, Professor of Geography, Portland State University

#5782. Democrats Are at COP31 to Show That the US Has Not Abandoned the Fight Against Climate Change

The results of the US midterms on November 3 delivered a resounding victory for the Democrats, and a major loss for US president Donald Trump and the Republican party.

Gaining control of the Senate and the House of Representatives has emboldened the Democrats, giving them a renewed sense of political legitimacy and a mandate to pursue their agenda. But will this shift translate into meaningful changes in US climate change policy?

The Democratic sweep will change the political dynamics around US climate policy and how the country cooperates with the international community on this issue. Although there was no official US presence at the 2025 COP conference, held in Brazil, a coalition of 100 local US leaders, including governors, mayors and other top city and state officials, attended as part of the US Climate Alliance. Former US vice-president Al Gore, and former US secretary of state John Kerry are part of an unofficial US group at the 2026 gathering.

Kerry said in a speech there: “Americans are committed to taking back their future, and we will build and rebuild our partnerships as we do that.”

Being on the ground at COP is important. As the US has a decisive role to play in global climate policy, sending a non-official coalition signals that many Americans are still working to combat climate change.

Trump has repeatedly stated that climate change is a hoax and refused to attend the COP31 climate talks being held in Turkey. But 20 Democratic members of Congress will be attending, although they have been denied official state department funding for the trip.

During the first and second Trump administrations, the US has been an outlier among wealthy countries when it comes to fighting climate change. Trump has actively backed the use of fossil fuels, undermining clean energy projects, and rolled back legislation that stipulated emission standards for vehicles.

Trump also weakened greenhouse gas reporting requirements and methane regulation. Then in February 2026, the Trump administration rescinded the Environmental Protection Agency’s 2009 finding that greenhouse gases threaten the health and welfare of the public, which had regulated the emissions from new cars and other vehicles. This had provided the legal foundation for regulation under the Clean Air Act.

On the international front, Trump was equally determined to undermine global efforts to fight climate change. Famously, he withdrew from the Paris agreement, part of a global initiative to address climate change, and refused to attend COP summits. But the Democrats’ seismic midterm win may be a sign of optimism for those fighting to address climate change.

The biggest issues of the midterms were affordability, corruption and the Iran war, but issues related to fighting climate change were also on voters’ list. There is growing concern about data centres. As many as 56% of US voters felt that data centres and AI were either a major or even crucial factor in influencing who they voted for, with only 13% saying it was not a factor at all.

Data centres require millions of gallons of water for cooling systems, and this is expected to rise to 73 billion litres of water a year by 2028. Over half of planned AI facilities in the US will be situated in areas that have significant water shortages or drought conditions.

After the midterms, Zoe Lofgren, a Democrat, is likely to become the chair of the House of Representatives’ committee on science, space and technology once the new session starts in January. She wants to tackle the administration’s “climate denialism”.

Lofgren’s leadership, along with new Democratic members of the committee, may offer it more power to reverse some of the Trump administration’s changes to science policy.

However, the Democrat midterm wins will not mean that the US is automatically back at the negotiating table at COP nor that the US will be able to rejoin the Paris Accords while Trump is president. Trump still has the power to make these decisions and can continue to keep the US out of international climate initiatives, regardless of who controls Congress. The US Constitution says nothing about withdrawing from treaties, which creates uncertainty for what the Senate’s role might be.

The election, however, does signal that there is considerable domestic opposition to his approach. And while Congress has not passed follow-up legislation prohibiting presidential withdrawal from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), it has continued to fund several UNFCCC initiatives. During the Biden administration, the US significantly increased climate finance from US$1.5 billion (£1.1 billion) a year in 2021 to US$9.5 billion in 2023.

Democrats could also push back on Trump’s current policies, using their power to hold hearings, investigate the administration’s dismantling of climate programmes and challenge cuts to scientific research. The Democrats can also use the power of Congress’s control of spending to protect or restore funding to some of these environmental initiatives.

They could also try to introduce legislation that reinstates some of the clean energy initiatives that had been implemented in past administrations to strengthen emissions standards and support clean energy. The big issue, however, is that Trump has made it clear that he is going to be very active in using his veto power, and without a two-thirds majority in Congress, the Democrats will not be able to override this.

What this all means is that the world cannot expect the US to be a reliable and constructive partner at COP with Trump still in power. Trump will probably continue to forge ahead with expanding fossil fuel production, while weakening international climate cooperation, even if the electorate disapproves of these policies.

Ironically, Trump’s greatest contribution to the fight against climate change was his initiation of the war with Iran, which helped to cut global fossil fuel carbon dioxide emissions by 0.4% due the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But climate scientists note this is not a long-term solution.

While the Democrats’ electoral victory offers a glimmer of hope for renewed climate action, both domestically and internationally, restoring US climate leadership will take time, especially while Trump remains in power.

By Natasha Lindstaedt, Professor in the Department of Government, University of Essex

#5781. Over One-Third Of Audi Nuvolari Production Will Be Sold In The U.S.

The 2027 Audi Nuvolari isn't a successor to the R8 because whereas that supercar was mass-produced in the tens of thousands over 18 years and two generations, just 499 Nuvolaris will ever be made. Audi has now announced that 182 of those are earmarked for the U.S., which means 36.5% of all Nuvolaris will land stateside, or one in every 2.74 cars.

Each will go for an official starting price of $700,000 before destination or taxes, and U.S. deliveries are scheduled to start in the first half of 2028. That's almost twice as much money as the Lamborghini Temerario on which it's based, but the Lambo isn't limited production or quite as special. Despite the numbered production run and how this sort of car tends to sell out before the public even knows about it, Audi of America says there are still build slots available, as "orders continue to be accepted at authorized Audi dealerships throughout the United States for a limited time."

Sharing its powertrain with the Temerario, the Audi Nuvolari uses a twin-turbo 4.0-liter V8 and three axial-flux hybrid electric motors to make 987 horsepower combined. 0 to 60 mph happens in just 2.5 seconds, and its top speed stands at 217 mph. It's said to use Formula 1-derived tech — Audi is in F1 now, in case you forgot — in the hybrid energy management system, by-wire brakes, active aero, and launch control programming.

It's also a new luxury performance car that manages to look good and original without being "polarizing." It's brutalist and a departure from existing Audi styling, but most colleagues I've talked to about it view its design favorably. For what it's worth, I think it's hella cool, particularly from the rear three-quarter view. Audi says there are 50 gloss paint colors and over 10 matte finishes, but you can of course make it look however you want with Audi Exclusive. You can get Audi's first exposed carbon-fiber body on the Nuvolari, and on the inside there's dozens more options.

In any case, if you're in the States and have 700 grand to splash on a German supercar (or, let's be real, almost a million after accounting for options, fees and taxes), there's apparently still time to go to your local Audi dealership and put your name down for a Nuvolari. You'd be joining a small club that only 181 other Americans will be a part of.

#5780. GLP-1 Drugs Linked to Improved Survival After Liver Transplant

— Reasons for lower mortality risk weren't clear in retrospective study

Liver transplant patients who took a GLP-1 receptor agonist had a lower risk of death than those who weren't on a GLP-1 drug, according to a retrospective three-center cohort study.

Among 2,402 patients, those on GLP-1 receptor agonists after their transplant were 45% less likely to die over a median 3.9 years of follow-up (adjusted HR [aHR] 0.55, 95% CI 0.38-0.80, P=0.002). That mortality risk advantage held whether or not transplant patients had type 2 diabetes, though the protective effect was greater among those without diabetes.

A replication cohort of 1,443 liver transplant recipients drawn from a U.S. claims database mirrored those results, showing 45% and 55% lower post-transplant mortality risks linked with GLP-1 use in two analyses (aHRs 0.55 and 0.45), reported Zhihao Li, MD, of the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases annual Liver Meeting in Denver.

"Several points support a real effect here," Li said in a presentation at the meeting. "The results were replicated in an independent cohort, they're similar to what's been reported in other organ transplants, and there are plausible cardiovascular and anti-cancer pathways."

Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is on pace to become the leading cause of liver transplant in the U.S. While a transplant cures liver disease, it doesn't remove a patient's metabolic or metabolic-related risks, Li noted. GLP-1 drugs deliver cardiometabolic and kidney benefits for patients with liver disease, but their value among liver transplant patients isn't clear, he added.

The primary study cohort included adults who underwent a liver transplant between 2015 and 2025 at one of three Mayo Clinic sites. Patients' transplant indication was either metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) or another etiology with type 2 diabetes or a body mass index (BMI) of at least 30 kg/m2. The replication cohorts were drawn from claims data in the OptumLabs Data Warehouse.

Median patient age was 61.2 years, 65.4% were male, 77.5% were white, and the median Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD)-Na score was 20. More than one-third (35.5%) had a MASH or metabolic indication for liver transplant. All patients had metabolic risk factors before liver transplant. Most patients had type 2 diabetes (58.9%), hypertension (65.3%), or a BMI of at least 30 (64.8%).

Among the 841 transplant patients who took GLP-1 drugs, 72% started them after their transplants. Median time to first GLP-1 dose was 1.5 years after transplant, and the median time spent taking the drugs was 1.2 years. Those on GLP-1 drugs were more likely to have MASH, diabetes, hypertension, obesity, or to be on statin therapy.

GLP-1 drug use was associated with a 14.2% drop in LDL cholesterol, an 8.3% drop in total cholesterol, and a 2.6% decline in HbA1c. Body weight fell by 5% in the 2 years after patients started a GLP-1 agonist.

Despite those changes, the reasons for the lower mortality risks weren't clear, Li said. Those on GLP-1 drugs weren't significantly less likely than their non-GLP-1 drug counterparts to experience a major adverse cardiovascular event (aHR 1.03, 95% CI 0.56-1.92) or, specifically, myocardial infarction (aHR 0.78, 95% CI 0.29-2.09).

The same was true for major adverse kidney events, sustained estimated glomerular filtration rate decline of at least 40%, or kidney transplant after liver transplant, though trends favored use of GLP-1 drugs. Li noted that a possible signal emerged for kidney failure in favor of GLP-1 drugs, but the difference just missed significance (aHR 0.46, P=0.06).

Most people who die after a liver transplant have a functioning graft, Li noted. Instead, malignancies, cardiovascular events, infections, and renal failure account for the majority of post-transplant deaths. Transplant patients on GLP-1 drugs were less likely than nonusers to die from those non-liver causes, including cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events, malignancies, infections, or graft failure. "This helps explain the survival benefit we observed," he said.

Limitations included the study's lack of power to detect differences in major adverse cardiovascular or kidney events. The cause of death wasn't known in 23% of patients, and drug exposure was relatively short. Sicker transplant recipients started GLP-1 drugs less often, Li noted.

#5779. 1967 Ford Ranchero For Sale With 3,100 Miles Shown Is 351 V8 Swapped, Bright Red And Ready To Roll

I'm known around these parts as a ute fan. Any car you can dream up, I've probably come across it built into a ute, and I've almost certainly liked that version better than the original. Once in a while, though, we have to pay respects to the originators of the ute life — the El Caminos, the Holdens, and of course the ever-gorgeous Ford Rancheros. Take this one, for instance: A 351-swapped 1967 Fairlane Ranchero that's not a hideous restomod.

This Ranchero, while modified and maintained over the course of its life, is gloriously free from any terrible four-spoke steering wheels or gaudy blue LED gauges. It does have an air conditioning system of questionable provenance (the control/vent unit doesn't appear to be either the factory Ford in-dash option available in 1967 nor the period-appropriate round-vented dealer accessory) as well as a modern single-DIN radio, but those are welcome and unobtrusive changes — they don't distract from the classic character of the car. The wheels certainly do, but some five-spoke American Classics will fix that handily.

Under the hood, though, is the mod that really matters: The Ranchero's factory 289ci V8 engine and its associated three-speed manual gearbox have been replaced with a 351 ci V8 and a four on the floor (with a Hurst shifter, even). It's not technically a period-correct swap, as the 351 postdates this Ranchero by a couple of years, but it's close enough that I'll count it. Better than putting a Coyote under there and pretending that the Ford badging maintains the car's character.

This OEM-plus Ranchero is on Bring a Trailer right now at a bidding price of just $2,500, which falls firmly into "Amber wants this" territory. I'm going to need you all to bump that number up until this ute starts to look like more of a bad idea to me, or Jalopnik's local kei car and motorcycle girlie might just end up with a giant hunk of American muscle street-parked outside her apartment. #5778. The Trump Administration’s Pro-Cancer Agenda

Under Trump, Americans could face an extraordinary increase in exposure to cancer-causing toxics and radiation.

Over the nearly two years of President Donald Trump’s second term, his administration has taken more than 500 actions that harm public health or the environment. When faced with this onslaught of harm, it can be difficult to see the strategic agenda at play. However, NRDC’s new analysis reveals that the Trump administration is executing a sweeping and long planned—but quiet—government-wide campaign to dismember major programs that are intended to prevent exposure to cancer-causing toxics and radiation. In sum, this administration has reversed course: America’s government is no longer fighting a “War on Cancer” but fighting a “War to Promote Cancer.”

This is not an accident. Much of this campaign can be found throughout the Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 blueprint and has long been advocated for by industry. But a healthy life should not be treated as an obstacle to somebody else’s profit margin. The freedom to breathe clean air, drink safe water, eat safe food, work without needless exposure to carcinogens, and raise children without avoidable toxic risks should be among the most basic expectations of life in America. Americans should not have to wonder whether the water coming from their taps contains cancer-causing chemicals, whether the air they breathe carries toxic pollution from a nearby industrial facility, or whether going to work means being unnecessarily exposed to carcinogens.

Instead of ensuring these basic freedoms, the Trump administration is creating a system in which polluters are given greater leeway to expose everyone in the nation to cancer-causing toxics and radiation.

#5776. At $10,250, Could This 1995 Mercedes-Benz E320 Estate Bring Class To Car Line?

It's arguable that the W124-series was the last of the bank-vault-era Benzes. Today's Nice Price or No Dice E320 estate is one of the most desirable of those vaults to potentially invest in, and it has the rare third row. Let's see if its price tag has us opening up our hypothetical bank accounts.

Perhaps the polar opposite of a Mercedes of any era in build quality, safety, and engineering is the backyard-built kit car. Arising in the late 1950s and carrying through its heyday in the 1970s, home-built kit cars typically started with a donor chassis, often from an old Triumph or VW. A fresh fiberglass body gave that chassis new life, and the builder a sense of pride in creating a working, drivable car.

The Meyers Manx SR2 we looked at on Wednesday was an example—and an extremely rare one at that—of a '70s-era kit car. Created by industry legend Bruce Meyers, the SR2 proved to be his swan song, as his company folded shortly after its launch. That makes the small clutch of original SR2s (about 200 total) far more dear when they do come on the market. Our SR2 came with Corvair power and an interior ready for the next owner's taste in upholstery. At $17,000, however, that wasn't a winning combo. You all expected more for that amount and sent the Manx packing with a massive 93% 'No Dice' loss.

The closest today's 1995 Mercedes-Benz E320 Estate comes to a kit car is that it's the same model year Mercedes-Benz India, Ltd. began building similar models from knock-down kits at its Chakan assembly plant. This is also nearly the last year for the W124 series as a whole, as it was replaced, body style by body style, over the course of the next three years: 1995 (saloons), 1996 (estates), 1997 (coupes), and 1998 (cabriolets). Mercedes is nothing if not methodical.

This generation, which represents the facelifted version of the W124, was also the first to carry Mercedes' new naming convention of a class letter followed by a number indicating—sometimes only semi-accurately—engine displacement. The company has carried on this convention to this day. Because of that simple nomenclature, we can tell from the name that this is a mid-size E-Class (Executive class) model with a 3.2-liter engine. See? Easy-peasy.

That 3.2-liter engine is an M104.992 straight-six with double-overhead cams and four valves per cylinder. In North American guise, it produces a workmanlike 217 horsepower and 229 pound-feet of torque. As in all U.S.-bound cars, here it's matched with a five-speed 4G-Tronic automatic actuated through Mercedes' traditional pixelated snake shift gate.

According to the ad, this car has undergone significant repairs and maintenance over its 159,850 miles. The seller notes that under their ownership, they replaced the engine wiring harness, head and head gasket, radiator, and water pump. In addition, the car has a new climate control panel and has had two failed window regulators replaced. Other plusses include Continental tires with plenty of tread left and "flawlessly working" A/C.

We've been living with affordable hybrid vehicles for almost three decades now, but it's taken a surprisingly long time for some of the best-selling cars in the U.S. to go hybrid-only, even for models that have offered reliable hybrids for years. Toyota started doing it with the current Camry and new RAV4, and now Honda has confirmed that the next-gen CR-V will only be sold with hybrid powertrains.

Honda says the seventh-generation CR-V will be revealed next year, in time for the SUV's 30th anniversary, and it will ride on a new platform and use the company's new two-motor hybrid system, which our own Andy Kalmowitz got to try out in a Civic prototype last year. This new powertrain is said to be more powerful and more efficient, and the modular architecture is more rigid while being lighter-weight. It should be cheaper for Honda to produce, too, and a new electric all-wheel-drive system will be a big improvement.

Somehow we didn't get a hybrid CR-V in the U.S. until the 2020 model year, when the fifth-gen model was facelifted. Since then, annual CR-V hybrid sales have grown almost tenfold, and it currently makes up more than 50% of total CR-V sales. With the price difference between the hybrid and the regular CR-V being so relatively minor, and the gains in driving experience being so large, it makes sense to just hybridize the entire lineup. This year will be the third straight year in which Honda sells more than 400,000 CR-Vs, and upping the average efficiency of that many cars can make a big difference.

Many U.S.-spec CR-Vs are currently built in Ohio (the rest being made in Indiana), and Honda just announced plans for a new $3 billion plant in Ohio that will focus on hybrids, though gas-only and fully electric cars will be built there as well. Production there won't start until 2029, but Honda envisions an annual capacity of 240,000 units. Honda says it will introduced 15 new hybrids by 2030, most of which will be oriented towards the American market.

One of those hybrids will be the model at the top of this slide, or at least something similar to it. That rakish fastback is officially called the Hybrid Sedan Prototype, and it's probably just the next-gen Accord that's due to come out in the very near future. It wears what will be Honda's new design language, and you don't have to imagine how it'll look on the CR-V — lightly camouflaged prototypes have already been spied, as you can see from the Instagram post below.

I think it's looking pretty good, though it's a shame that the CR-V will seemingly lose its signature vertical taillights. We probably won't have to wait long to see the CR-V; expect an actual auto show debut, simply because a car this popular can actually take the spotlight and be of interest to the regular people who still go to shows. A Detroit Auto Show debut in January seems like a safe bet, but Honda could wait for Chicago in February or New York in March.

#5773. The High-Rise Bottleneck: Why EV Charging in Indian Apartments Is an Engineering Puzzle

Most Western clean-energy reporting takes a very specific picture of home charging for granted. You pull into a private driveway, plug into an attached garage wall-box, and pull cheap power while you sleep.

That reality does not exist for most urban drivers in India.

Data from Kazam and the Alliance for an Energy Efficient Economy (AEEE) shows that roughly 70% to 75% of urban households in major Indian metros live in multi-family apartments and cooperative housing societies. Parking means an open ground level slot or a space two levels down in a concrete basement. When someone here buys an electric car, their biggest hurdle isn’t battery degradation or highway chargers. It’s their own building.

As an electrical engineer in India, I watch this play out every week. Someone buys an EV, assumes they can hire a local wireman to pull power from their flat’s meter to their parking bay, and runs straight into transformer limits, cable physics, and nervous managing committees.

Here is what is actually going on beneath the floorboards.

Indian housing societies buy electricity under a bulk “sanctioned load” from their local utility (DISCOM). The utility sizes the local transformer using an electrical diversity factor the simple assumption that not all 100 flats will run their air conditioners, geysers, and induction stoves at the exact same moment.

A domestic geyser pulls 2 kW for ten minutes and shuts off. A 7.4 kW AC wall-box pulls 32 amps continuously for six to eight hours. When several residents plug in around 8:00 PM, that heavy, unbroken draw lands on the transformer right as domestic air conditioning and kitchen loads hit their evening peak.

Let’s look at the numbers on a 100-flat complex running on a standard 250 kVA transformer:

Here is where the grid cracks: just five or six cars charging at 7.4 kW pull 37 kW to 44 kW. That wipes out the 30 kW buffer completely. If eight cars plug in at once (59.2 kW), the transformer goes straight into thermal overload.

When that happens, the main incomer breaker trips plunging common areas and elevators into darkness or the utility slaps the society with massive Maximum Demand penalties on their next power bill. Getting a utility to upgrade a transformer or approve higher sanctioned load requires significant capital, transformer yard space, and months of red tape.

In a detached house, wiring an EV charger means running 5 or 10 metres of cable from your distribution board to the garage.

In an Indian high-rise, your electricity meter sits in a ground-floor panel room or inside a service shaft on the 14th floor. Your car is parked two floors beneath the earth in Basement 2. Connecting the two is an expensive engineering problem:

Even if an owner is willing to foot the entire wiring bill, they still need a No Objection Certificate (NOC) from their housing society committee or Resident Welfare Association (RWA).

Most RWA committees are volunteer residents without technical backgrounds. When handed a request for high-power continuous charging, their hesitation usually comes down to three worries:

The courts are starting to step in. In Amit Dholakia v. The State of Maharashtra (2025), the Bombay High Court pushed state authorities to issue clear guidelines preventing arbitrary NOC rejections. More recently, in early 2026, the Supreme Court of India issued notice on a Public Interest Litigation challenging arbitrary charger bans across states. While the legal momentum is clearly moving toward protecting a resident’s right to charge, taking a court ruling to a heated Sunday morning society meeting rarely makes for a quick installation.

Treating an electric car like an extra microwave where everyone pulls their own line from their domestic meter does not scale. Societies have to build shared electrical infrastructure.

India’s EV transition is moving fast on two and three wheels. But passenger electric cars won’t reach mass adoption until high-rises solve the overnight charging puzzle.

The vehicles are ready, and buyers want them. But until building codes, dynamic load balancing, and society committees catch up with automotive engineering, the hardest part of driving electric in India will simply be charging at home.

#5772. Perioperative Therapy Tops Prostatectomy Alone in High-Risk Prostate Cancer

— PROTEUS substudy shows a 62% lower risk of recurrence or death with apalutamide plus ADT

Results from a substudy of the phase III PROTEUS trial presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) congress showed that adding apalutamide (Erleada) and androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) before and after radical prostatectomy reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 62% compared with prostatectomy alone in patients with high-risk localized prostate cancer.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, Mary-Ellen Taplin, MD, of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston, discusses the findings.

Following is a transcript of her remarks:

At ASCO 2026 in the plenary, the PROTEUS main study was presented, which was a very large, 2,100-patient study, which looked at the effect of 6 months of neoadjuvant apalutamide and ADT compared to placebo and ADT, followed by prostatectomy. And then everyone received another 6 months of the therapy they had been assigned to. So that study was positive. It showed a 20% reduction in metastasis or death by central imaging review and a 26% reduction by investigator assessment.

And to complement that data, there was a substudy done, which was what was presented at ESMO during one of the oral sessions. So the substudy compared what I'll refer to as the PROTEUS regimen, so 6 months of ADT and apalutamide before and after prostatectomy to standard-of-care prostatectomy alone. There was a 3:1 randomization to the prostatectomy alone to obtain more patients for a comparison to the prostatectomy.

So the primary endpoint of the substudy was a little bit different than the primary endpoints of the main study. So the main study had two co-primary endpoints, which was pathologic response and MFS (metastasis-free survival). The primary endpoint of the substudy was event-free survival at 3 years. So event-free survival includes relapse by any means -- so PSA [prostate-specific antigen], local recurrence, [and] imaging relapse, which included PSMA [prostate-specific membrane antigen] PET or conventional imaging.

So this primary endpoint was very, very positive. There was a 62% reduction in the risk of recurrence or death with the 6 months of apalutamide and ADT before and after surgery, prostatectomy. And this was true controlling over time for the analysis at the longer time points when accounting for testosterone recovery. In addition, there was a 51% lower risk of death or metastasis -- again, metastasis by PSMA PET or conventional imaging. Fifty percent fewer patients received subsequent therapy at all by 3 years. And importantly, there was a 50% reduction in any radiation after receiving the neoadjuvant ADT and apalutamide. So in summary, the primary endpoint, event-free survival, and all the secondary endpoints including MFS and first subsequent therapy were all very positive for the combined neoadjuvant apalutamide, ADT, and prostatectomy.

Safety is very important to assess. The main side effects were similar, I would say, to what is known for apalutamide and ADT. Can't be ignored, but in general are easily managed in the clinic and include fatigue, hot flashes, and incidence of rash. The rash with apalutamide is different than a rash say with antibiotics. It's less of an allergic type rash and more immune-mediated where patients can continue the drug with a dose reduction or a short interruption.

Hypertension is a known class side effect of androgen pathway receptor inhibitors. Importantly, there was no increase in surgical complications. This is a nice study designed to analyze that with the neoadjuvant and the adjuvant therapy combined with prostatectomy compared to prostatectomy alone.

Notably, to me, is that in the control arm the patients who had prostatectomy, 70% of patients relapsed by 3 years. So these are men who -- prostatectomies alone are not curing them, and they need subsequent therapy which may or may not put them into remission.

So I think that's important to take into consideration when thinking about the best treatments for patients. You have to dissect the pros and cons of surgery, androgen deprivation, and radiation, and think about the general health of your patient, their age, their goals. Is ADT and an androgen pathway inhibitor safe? And is surgery versus radiation safe? And those are the types of analyses that the treating physician needs to make when thinking about these patients with very high-risk localized prostate cancer.

#5771. What's The Worst Way You've Abused A Rental Car?

Unless you only travel within driving distance of home or are willing to spend the time and money on shipping, we will all end up in a situation where renting a car is a necessity. There may be plenty of cities with fantastic public transportation systems, but you just need a car to venture out and explore the countryside. Many of us are far more care-free behind the wheel when the vehicle is owned by an abstract corporate entity and not a person with a face.

What's the worst way you've abused a rental car? I'm not talking about returning it with an empty tank. That's just a surcharge that rental companies are more than happy to add to your bill. Abuse is real, lasting damage that's an absolute nightmare to reverse. Let me use a hypothetical beach day in the South of France as an example. You and a few friends take a decent Peugeot 408 to a sleepy village on the Mediterranean. After a fun day of sand and surf, everyone piles back into the sedan right off the beach, covering the interior with sand. That's the appetizer. On the drive back, you get impatient sitting behind a truck on a two-lane road. You pull into the oncoming lane but don't get entirely clear, and you sideswipe the truck. The 408 is far worse off, with its entire right side scratched up. That's abuse!

Besides outright crashing a rental car, the worst thing you could do is race a pack of them. Rental car racing actually is a significant part of NASCAR lore. The mischievous tradition has endured stock car racing's evolution from a moonshiners' pastime to a billion-dollar sport. Several current Cup Series drivers have admitted to racing each other and their team members. In many instances, rental car racing is just a fun way to salvage a rained-out test day. Everyone just piles on to the track once the showers stop and run laps to dry the racing surface. On race day, it's pushing the limit on the drive out of the track. Joe Gibbs Racing driver Chase Briscoe told The Athletic in 2025, "Honestly, the craziest thing, I think, is watching the team guys leave a racetrack. It is like the best racing and just the most chaos you've ever seen in your life."

#5767. Novel Sjogren's Drug Passes First Phase III Test

— Barring catastrophe in second trial, approval seems likely

ORLANDO -- An investigational CD40L antagonist called dazodalibep looks to be nearing the finish line on the way to approval for Sjögren's disease, based on results from a 48-week phase III trial reported here.

With scores on the EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Disease Activity Index (ESSDAI) as the randomized trial's primary outcome measure, patients on the active drug saw reductions of 5.2 and 5.6 points by week 48, depending on which of two doses they received, compared with a 3.8-point decline with placebo (P<0.05 and P<0.001, respectively), reported Ghaith Noaiseh, MD, of the University of Kansas in Kansas City.

Clinically significant reductions of 3 points were achieved by about two-thirds of patients receiving dazodalibep; fewer met more stringent response levels, but even so, fully half of patients on the higher of the two doses had ESSDAI scores drop by 7 points, Noaiseh said during a late-breaking abstract session at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting. Despite a strong placebo response in the trial, the drug held a statistically significant advantage.

In addition, safety findings were better than unremarkable, with fewer serious adverse events than were seen with placebo.

This was one of a pair of phase III trials conducted by drugmaker Amgen, which took control of dazodalibep when it bought the original developer, Horizon Therapeutics, in 2023. The other has not been completed but should be soon, the company has said. These studies follow encouraging results from phase II trials reported in 2023.

Dazodalibep is intended to disrupt interaction between the CD40 receptor and its ligand, CD40L, which should have a wide range of effects, Noaiseh explained. It "disrupts CD40L-mediated costimulatory interactions between T cells, B cells, glandular epithelial cells, and other antigen-presenting cells," he said. That leads to decreased production of inflammatory mediators as well as autoantibodies.

Also of note, although it's a biologic drug, it's not a monoclonal antibody -- rather, it's a fusion product based on an antibody but with the Fc portion removed, Noaiseh said, noting that previous efforts to target CD40L with an antibody led to unacceptably high rates of thrombosis.

For this first phase III study, the investigators enrolled 648 Sjögren's disease patients, randomizing them to three arms: placebo, dazodalibep 3,000 mg every 12 weeks (low dose), or the drug at 1,500 mg every 4 weeks (high dose). Their mean age was 53, and 94% were women. Some 56% were from Europe and North America, 7% from Japan, and the rest from a variety of other countries.

Baseline ESSDAI scores averaged 10.2, with about 20% having scores of 14 or higher, indicating high activity. A key secondary outcome measure was the EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Patient-Reported Index (ESSPRI); scores at baseline averaged 7.07. Another outcome that was developed specially for these trials was a Diary for Assessing Sjögren's Patients Index (DASPRI), in which patients recorded their symptoms daily, including dryness at four separate body locations -- a complement to ESSPRI, which asks patients about symptoms during the previous 2 weeks and only rates overall dryness.

In general, the higher dazodalibep dose was more effective. This was most clearly seen in data on dryness, with a decrease of 2.5 points on ESSPRI's dryness domain, and a 1.98-point decrease in DASPRI dryness -- compared with -1.33 and -1.05 with placebo, respectively (P<0.001 for both comparisons). Dryness relief with the lower drug dose came in about halfway between the high dose and placebo, missing statistical significance.

Overall rates of treatment-emergent adverse events were similar across all three arms, affecting some 85% of patients. Those considered treatment-related were a bit more common with the high-dose drug (37% vs 25% for placebo), but only five events were rated as serious in the entire study sample, two of which were in the placebo group. Likewise, discontinuations because of adverse events were about the same in the three arms, with 24 total among the 648 participants.

The investigators also examined "special interest" events that could potentially arise from this novel biologic agent targeting a range of immune functions. These included allergic and hypersensitivity reactions, thromboembolism, opportunistic infections, and various malignancies. There were very few of any of these, and none were more common with either dazodalibep dose versus placebo. In total, 40 such events were seen, including 14 with placebo, 12 in the low-dose group, and 14 with the high dose.

Nvidia was already spinning up investigations when that news broke, but new reporting alleges Huang also cheated with an employee at the company — one who reported to Huang himself. Now, Huang is out, and Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is in the CEO chair in an interim role. From Nvidia:

NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.

Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.

Huang cofounded Nvidia, but he doesn't seem as integral to its operations as, say, Elon Musk is to SpaceX. The bigger issue Nvidia is facing right now is a lack of clear successorship, with no one sitting as heir apparent to the top spot — Huang planned to run the company himself for decades more before ever thinking of leaving, and he didn't exactly prepare anyone to take his place.

Kress, the CFO, is a logical interim replacement for the state of Nvidia right now: A financial house of cards built on circular financing and impossible valuations, moreso than a creator of cutting-edge computing hardware. What happens next, though — to both NVIDIA's automotive chipsets and its role in AI — is anyone's guess.

EV sales are rough in the U.S. right now, and growth in China has tapered off. European sales, though, are still growing — and they're bringing the world up with them. Sales are climbing, despite our intent to go as backwards as possible. From Reuters:

Nov 12 (Reuters) – Global demand for electrified cars returned to growth in October, reflecting a very low ​US comparison base coupled with continued growth in ‌Europe, data from UK-based research firm Benchmark Mineral Intelligence showed on Thursday.

"Even though the Chinese market is down domestically, that has ​then in turn resulted in a lot of ​OEMs pushing the exports and contributing significantly to ⁠the rest of the world," Benchmark data manager ​Charles Lester told Reuters.

* Global sales of new battery-electric and plug-in ​hybrid electric vehicles climbed 8% from a year ago to 2.09 million vehicles in October, while year-to-date volumes were up 5% at ​17.5 million units

It's going to be very interesting to see what happens with U.S. EVs over the next couple of years. Will the midterm "blue wave" propel us to government funding for EV infrastructure?

Honda wants to grow sales in the U.S., despite buyers' financial struggles, but it has a plan for how to marry those factors: Hybrids. The company thinks that, by making cars that save you on fuel, it'll make you more likely to spend upfront for one. From Automotive News:

Honda, aided by a $3 billion assembly plant planned for central Ohio, is striving to boost U.S. sales 17 percent within five years.

Honda retailers who attended the meeting at Resorts World Las Vegas got a preview of a handful of new and updated models arriving in the next several years, including the highly anticipated overhaul of the top-selling CR-V crossover and the return of a cult favorite, the Element. Dealers who spoke to Automotive News asked not to be identified while discussing information shared at the event.

I love a hybrid, so I can't wait for a hybrid Element. Sure, it won't be quite as simple as the outgoing one, but I'm excited to take one rock climbing anyway. Hopefully Honda keeps the doors right, at least.

The Fiat 500 is a fun little car, but we're not much in an era of fun little cars at the moment. As such, demand is low, and the Fiat 500 is selling so slowly as to make Stellantis idle its Italian manufacturing plant. From Reuters:

Stellantis' historic Mirafiori plant in northern Italy, which makes the Fiat 500 city car, will remain shut ​next week, extending a production halt into a fifth ‌week, unions said on Thursday.

Igor Albera, from the ⁠FIM-CISL union, told Reuters that the prolonged production stoppages ​at the Turin plant were due in part to component shortages ​and in part to weak demand for the model

You'd think, with wages stagnating as costs increase, that people would return to cheap small cars. Have we really ceded so much of our souls to the C-HRs of the world that there's no room left for the humble Fiat 500?

"I lift my lamp beside where the golden door used to be" just doesn't hit the same.

At this point, Jensen probably wishes it was just a pretty little souped up four-wheel-drive.

#5764. QuantumScape Has An Osprey Up Its Solid-State EV Battery Sleeve

Federal policy makers orchestrated an EV sales crash in the US last year, only to see electrification stakeholders gradually piece together a comeback focusing on cars that hit the affordability MSRP of $30,000 or less. New, higher-performing solid-state EV batteries are also inching their way towards the market, with the US startup QuantumScape among the innovators contributing some fresh news in recent weeks (for the record, Finland’s Donut Labs is another).

As the name indicates, a solid-state battery replaces the liquid electrolyte of a conventional lithium-ion battery with a solid material. If that sounds like a deep electrochemical challenge, its is. Nevertheless, science loves a challenge, and so do electrification stakeholders who are determined to sharpen the contrast between EVs and gasmobiles. Compared to the current generation of EV batteries, solid-state technology meets a higher bar for energy density and other performance benchmarks, while avoiding the use of volatile chemicals (see more solid-state background here)

High tech ceramics have emerged as one of the options, and that is where QuantumScape has set its sights. The company launched in 2010 and it surfaced on the CleanTechnica radar in 2012, when Volkswagen dropped word of its interest in the solid-state forumula.

QS has been focusing its attention on developing a lithium-metal formula for the anode (the part of a battery that collects a charge), by tweaking the separator, which is the part of a battery that serves as a buffer on the electrolyte.

“A solid-state lithium-metal battery…replaces the polymer separator used in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a solid-state separator. The replacement of the separator enables the carbon or silicon anode used in conventional lithium-ion batteries to be replaced with a lithium-metal anode,” QS explains.

To ice the solid-state cake, the QS anode does not make an appearance during the battery manufacturing process. It self-forms as part of the battery’s first charging cycle.

QS has accumulated a string of investors and affiliations since 2012, capped by a hookup with the legacy firm Corning last year aimed at developing a manufacturing system that accommodates its ceramic separator.

The latest news takes QS farther into all-solid state technology, this time with a focus on the cathode, under the trade name Osprey.

“Osprey pairs the QS proprietary ceramic separator and anode-free lithium-metal design with a solid cathode, creating an all-solid-state cell,” the company explained in a press statement on November 11.

“Osprey builds on the company’s QSE platform, and opens new licensing and co-development options for current QS customers and expanding its offering to developers of sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries,” the company elaborates. The QS blog further explains that Osprey is a “solid-state platform that allows developers of sulfide-based solid-state batteries to incorporate QS technology into their all-solid-state battery (ASSB) development programs.”

Don’t get too excited just yet — the cathode work is still in the early stages of validation — but QS is now confident that its data will stand up under public scrutiny. In addition to safety improvements compared to conventional Li-ion batteries, QS checks a list of additional performance boxes for ASSBs:

“Cycle life: 1,000 full charge cycles with ~80% capacity retention under gold-standard testing conditions

Fast charging: 10% to 80% in five-minutes

Low pressure: Requires only one atmosphere of pressure

Cold-weather performance: Operational to less than -20 °C (-4 °F)

Want more details? Check out the QS blog, where the company takes a deeper dive into the new cathode.

As for why QS is working the sulfide angle, that’s a good question. “Sulfides can react with lithium metal, which shortens battery life, and they typically need to be held under high pressure to operate, which is impractical for vehicles and many other applications,” QS notes. Despite those challenges, QS also notes the sulfide formula continues to attract widespread interest in the solid-state field, due to its high level of conductivity and ease of processing. If all goes according to plan, the Osprey platform will enable solid-state battery developers to continue pursuing sulfide to their hearts’ content.

“The industry has invested heavily in sulfide-based batteries but keeps hitting the same fundamental limits,” explains QS president and CEO Dr. Siva Sivaram, “As the data shows, Osprey can address these limitations.”

As another indication that sulfide stakeholders are not out chasing rainbows, take a look at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, part of a sprawling network of research facilities under the umbrella of the US Department of Energy. ORNL has just published a new study in the journal Energy Materials under the title, “Operando neutron radiography reveals calendar aging-induced lithium redistribution and back-diffusion in thick-cathode all-solid-state batteries.”

As the title indicates, the researchers deployed a neutron radiation tool to probe the inner workings of lithium batteries while they are in operation, enabling them to deliver a precise map of the degradation process that has bedeviled the sulfide field. They also delivered a roadmap for further work:

“Based on these findings from calendar aging, we envision future formation strategies should be redesigned to minimize sustained potential gradients while stabilizing interphases, for example through optimized composite electronic percolation and catholyte or coating materials and validated with time-resolved neutron imaging to establish transport-informed, durability-first conditioning rules that generalize across cathode loadings and operating temperatures.”

Got all that? The real question is why a federal research institution is still delivering advanced analyses leading to the next generation of EV batteries that outperform conventional batteries while improving EV safety and reducing overall costs. After all, US President Donald Trump and the Republican majority in Congress have expended considerable time and effort to stop, if not reverse, EV sales in the US. In addition to prematurely killing off the $7,500 EV tax credit last fall, the President also tried (and ultimately failed) to claw back funds from the federal NEVI public EV charging station program.

Readers, take a guess at the answer in the discussion thread. One possible explanation is the energy storage angle. While the President’s whackadoodle “American Energy Dominance Policy” dials down solar and wind (especially wind), it supports practically every other domestic energy resource including nuclear, biomass, geothermal, and hydropower alongside fossil fuels, with energy storage also making a substantial appearance.

The electronic war of the future is another factor to consider, with crewless vehicles and “anti-idling” kits serving as a sort of gateway drug that demonstrates the logistical and tactical advantages of battery power, silent running, and a lower heat signature compared to diesel fuel.

Photo: The US startup Quantumscape is contributing its new “Osprey” platform to kickstart solid-state EV batteries into the mass market and help accelerate the vehicle electrification movement (screenshot courtesy of QS via YouTube).

#5763. Novel GLP-1 Cut Heavy Drinking Days in Alcohol Use Disorder

— 42% of patients on pemvidutide achieved zero heavy drinking days by week 24

The investigational glucagon/GLP-1 dual receptor agonist pemvidutide significantly reduced the number of heavy drinking days (HDDs) per week in patients with moderate-to-severe alcohol use disorder (AUD), the phase II RECLAIM trial showed.

After 24 weeks of treatment, HDDs per week decreased by 4.20 days with pemvidutide versus 2.75 days with placebo (P=0.0014), reported Henry R. Kranzler, MD, of the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, during the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases annual meeting in Denver.

In addition, more patients receiving the drug achieved zero HDDs by week 24 (42.2% vs 17.4% with placebo; OR 3.8, 95% CI 1.4-10.4, P=0.0066), as well as higher rates of ≥2-level WHO Risk Drinking Levels (64.4% vs 34.8%; OR 3.3, 95% CI 1.4-7.7, P=0.0049).

"In the context of alcohol use disorder -- which can be a life-threatening condition -- the positive effects are meaningful, and the adverse events are tolerable," Kranzler told MedPage Today.

Of note, patients on pemvidutide also achieved reductions in serum phosphatidylethanol (PEth) levels compared with increases in the placebo group (least-squares mean change from baseline -153.4 ng/mL vs +22.0 ng/mL, P<0.0001).

PEth is a "highly sensitive, highly specific measure of alcohol consumption that doesn't depend on self-reporting, and is objective," Kranzler said, adding that pemvidutide showed a "very robust" effect on PEth, while the placebo group showed a small increase, "which suggests that they were reporting greater reductions in drinking than they were actually experiencing."

"Even though the primary outcome was [a reduction in heavy drinking days], I'm most impressed by the PEth findings," he noted.

According to the 2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health, 57.9 million current alcohol users ages 12 and older engaged in binge drinking in the past month, while 27.9 million had AUD in the past year. Excessive alcohol use leads to 178,000 deaths annually, with about one-third from binge drinking.

While the FDA has approved three therapies to treat AUD, only a small percentage of people with the disorder access these drugs.

Pemvidutide has balanced 1:1 glucagon/GLP-1 dual receptor agonist activity that reduces liver fat, inflammation, and fibrosis. A previous phase IIb trial showed that pemvidutide led to resolution of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) without worsening of fibrosis, but did not improve fibrosis without worsening of MASH.

Studies of other GLP-1 receptor agonists have shown that they reduce drinking in people with AUD, and there's also evidence that they affect the reward system in the brain, in addition to having peripheral effects in the gastrointestinal tract.

Thus, this study in AUD was a "logical next step," Kranzler said.

In RECLAIM, 100 patients with moderate-to-severe AUD were randomized to receive subcutaneous pemvidutide or placebo once weekly for 24 weeks, together with a standardized behavioral intervention.

Participants had to be engaging in heavy drinking (28 drinks per week for men, 21 for women) with at least 3 HDDs per week (≥5 drinks per day for men, ≥4 for women) over 28 days prior to screening.

Mean age was about 50, 52% were women, mean body mass index was about 32, and roughly 75% were categorized as having severe AUD. The average number of HDDs per week was 5.6 in the placebo group and 5.9 in the pemvidutide group.

Of the 100 participants randomized, 78% and 80% in the placebo and pemvidutide groups, respectively, completed treatment, while 92% and 90% completed the study.

More participants in the pemvidutide group versus the placebo group had an increase in percent days abstinent (38.9% vs 20.5%, P=0.0075) and the drug led to a higher numerical reduction in the number of drinks per drinking day (-4.9 vs -3.8), though this was not significant.

Pemvidutide also led to reductions in body weight (percent change -8.7% vs +0.4%, P<0.0001) and Fibrosis-4 scores (-0.3 vs +0.2, P=0.0301).

Overall, the most common adverse events (AEs) were mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal events (62% in the pemvidutide group and 34% in the placebo group).

Serious AEs occurred in two patients in the pemvidutide group (including a patient with hyponatremia possibly related to the drug) and one patient in the placebo group.

There were three severe AEs related to pemvidutide (including the patient with hyponatremia, one patient with migraine, and one with fatigue, night sweats, nausea, and gastroesophageal reflux disease).

Drug-related AEs leading to treatment discontinuation occurred in 10% of patients in the pemvidutide group.

#5762. A BMW i3 Spent Less Than 3 Hours Charging On A 3,658-Mile Road Trip, Is That Fast Enough For You?

Regardless of how you feel about the exterior styling, interior design, infotainment software, or even driving dynamics of BMW's latest Neue Klasse models, there's no denying the new electric cars are extremely impressive when it comes to range, efficiency and charging. The in-demand Neue Klasse cars have consistently outperformed in real-world range tests, and last year BMW drove an iX3 from Debrecen, Hungary, to Munich, Germany, covering 626 miles on a single charge.

To show off just how road-trip-capable its Neue Klasse cars are, BMW took the new i3 on the Paneuropeana, a long-distance EV rally route devised by Rafael de Mestre, who has circumnavigated the globe in electric cars four times. The car covered 5,886.7 kilometers on the journey, or 3,658 miles rounded up — over 1,000 miles more than you'd drive when crossing the United States. It took 3 days, 2 hours and 41 minutes to complete the drive, and only 2 hours and 46 minutes was spent charging. Is that fast enough for you, yet?

The trip started at the North Cape in Norway, the northernmost point of continental Europe that you can get to by car (about 1,300 miles from the North Pole), and after crossing through eight countries ended in Tarifa, the southernmost point of Europe in the Andalusian region of Spain. Along the way they encounted bad weather and rough roads, so it wasn't a walk in the park. The focus of the drive isn't outright speed, so the checkpoints and stages are organized like "regular road users travelling along country roads, motorways and through towns," according to BMW.

Charging stops weren't pre-determined, though, and BMW says that made for a great challenge: "optimising the route between checkpoints specifically to make the best use of the charging infrastructure, whilst also taking into account external factors such as the weather, traffic jams, etc." The charging stations chosen were public ones, adding to the potential issues. In the video covering the trip, at one point the team got the car down to 0% with 0 kilometers of range left, and in another moment they arrive at a high-power charging station to find no chargers working.

Only one engineer was in the i3 at any given time, with the car being followed by an identical i3 and an iX3 for support. The i3 in question was a 50 xDrive model, which has a 108.7-kWh battery pack, a dual-motor powertrain with 463 horsepower, and an EPA-rated range of up to 468 miles in the States (567 miles on the European WLTP cycle).

The point of the Paneuropeana is to see who can spend the least amount of time charging along the route, and BMW broke the record by more than seven hours. The i3 can charge at up to 400 kW, and on the trip BMW saw an average charging power of 275 kW, which ain't bad. BMW says the i3's average speed was just about 50 mph, and its energy consumption was damn impressive: 12.5 kWh per 100 km, which translates to almost 5 miles per kWh in U.S. figures. That's better efficiency than the i3's WLTP rating.

BMW hasn't said how many times the i3 stopped to charge, or how long the average stop was, but does that really matter? A U.S.-spec i3 can gain 180 miles of range in just 10 minutes of charging, and it can go from 10% to 80% in 21 minutes. At steady highway speeds, the i3 should be able to take you almost 400 miles before needing to be juiced up again. That's got to be good enough to assuage any range anxiety you've still got kicking around in your brain.

#5761. OEDRO Car Accessories Fix Common Family Road Trip Interior Problems for SUV & Pickup Owners

Planning a family road trip usually starts with excitement. Everyone gets involved in choosing the destination, checking the route, preparing snacks, and packing luggage for the journey. Parents make sure the kids have entertainment, while other family members prepare drinks, travel essentials, and everything needed for a comfortable ride. However, amid all the preparation, some easily overlooked vehicle interior problems can turn into unexpected inconveniences along the way. A little mud brought into the cabin, difficulty climbing into a tall pickup, or small belongings scattered across the seats may not seem like serious issues before departure. Yet after several hours on the road, these minor problems can become frustrating, particularly when traveling with children or older family members. A comfortable road trip is not only about reaching the destination; it is also about making sure everyone can enjoy the journey without constantly dealing with unnecessary mess and discomfort.

Family travel puts a vehicle’s interior to the test. One of the most common challenges is keeping the floor clean. Children may step into the vehicle with muddy shoes after outdoor activities, while food crumbs, spilled drinks, and snack wrappers can quickly make the factory carpet look messy. Cleaning these stains can take time, especially after a long trip. Another issue is getting in and out of taller SUVs and pickup trucks. Although their higher ground clearance is useful for different driving conditions, the height can make entry and exit less convenient for young children and older passengers. Repeatedly climbing into the cabin may require extra effort and assistance. Finally, there is the problem of small items getting everywhere. Toys, charging cables, tissues, water bottles, and travel accessories often end up under seats or scattered around the cabin. When passengers cannot find what they need, the journey can become less organized. These problems may be ordinary, but addressing them before departure can make a noticeable difference to the overall travel experience.

A few practical interior upgrades can help address these common challenges without requiring major vehicle modifications. First, custom-fit TPE floor mats provide an additional layer of protection against dirt, mud, and everyday spills. Their molded design helps contain mess within the mat area, making cleanup more manageable after outdoor stops or busy family trips. For example, the OEDRO all-weather TPE floor mats for 2023–2025 Honda CR-V models, including Hybrid are designed for compatible vehicle interiors.

Second, running boards can make entering and exiting a taller vehicle more convenient. They provide a stepping surface along the side of the truck, giving passengers an additional point of support when getting into the cabin. The OEDRO running boards for 2015–2020 Ford F-150 SuperCrew are one option for owners of compatible models.

Third, under-seat storage boxes help keep smaller travel essentials in one designated place. Instead of leaving toys, tools, and other belongings scattered around the cabin, drivers can use otherwise overlooked space beneath the seats. The OEDRO 2-in-1 storage box for compatible Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra models offers a practical way to organize items while making better use of available cabin space. Always check the product’s listed vehicle compatibility before ordering.

These accessories do not change a vehicle’s engine performance, horsepower, or driving capability. Their value lies in improving the everyday experience of using the vehicle, particularly when several passengers and plenty of belongings are involved. Floor mats help reduce the amount of dirt and moisture reaching the original carpet, making post-trip cleanup less demanding. Running boards offer a more convenient stepping point for passengers, which can be especially helpful for children and older family members when entering or leaving a taller vehicle. Meanwhile, storage boxes help prevent small belongings from taking over the cabin, allowing passengers to find their essentials more easily. Together, these upgrades support a cleaner, more accessible, and better-organized interior. They can also help drivers spend less time tidying up after every stop and more time enjoying the trip with their families. Of course, passengers should still use appropriate care when stepping onto running boards, and all loose items should be stored securely before driving. A little preparation can go a long way toward making long journeys feel more relaxed.

A successful family road trip involves more than choosing the right destination and packing enough snacks. The condition and organization of your vehicle’s interior also play an important role in keeping everyone comfortable throughout the journey. Whether you want to protect your carpet from muddy shoes, make it easier for passengers to enter a taller pickup, or keep everyday travel essentials from getting lost beneath the seats, choosing accessories that suit your vehicle can help solve these everyday problems. #5758. I Have A 100 Mile Commute Through Mountain Roads! What Car Should I Buy?

David works as a firefighter in Seattle but lives about 100 miles outside the in the mountains. He needs a comfortable, reliable, and practical vehicle with all-weather capability. With a budget up to $30,000, what car should he buy?

(Welcome back to What Car Should You Buy? Where we give real people real advice about buying cars. Do you want us to help you find a car? Submit your story on our form.)

I have a 100 mile (each way) mountain pass commute from Leavenworth to the Seattle area. I need a fuel efficient (or electric??) car that can haul lots of gear, run to the hardware store, seat at least 5 (6 would be awesome), AWD or 4x4, and be fun on twisty mountain roads. Open to auto or manual transmission. Budget is about $30,000

I'm sure the fuel costs on that 100-mile commute really eat into your paycheck: If you were averaging 30 mpg in a gas car that works out roughly to $680/month in gas. You mentioned being open to an EV and I assume you would have charging access at home and/or work. Not only will an electric car save you a lot of money on fuel, they are statistically more reliable than their gas counterparts.

Now that more folks are catching on to EVs, the value propositions at that $30,000 mark are reducing but there are still several good options available. You like your Toyotas and the bZ4X (co-created with Subaru) is pretty easy to come by at that price point. While these aren't the most impressive EVs, they do the job, have room for five, and will keep your running costs down. The caveat is that AWD versions have a maximum range of about 288 miles, so charging to 80% and factoring in cold-weather range reduction could be an issue. Here is a nice example with reasonable miles for just under $25,000

You know, David, a lot of the letters we get for What Car Should You Buy? have a pretty obvious solution. Or several obvious solutions. In those cases, the challenge is finding something a little less obvious, because it would get boring fast if every WCSYB answer was just the most obvious picks. You, on the other hand, seem to need a plug-in hybrid sports car that's also a work truck. They don't really make those, and I have a feeling both the Hyundai Santa Cruz and Ford Maverick will be too small for five fully grown firefighters and their gear. So we're going to have to look elsewhere.

Since there aren't any perfect options, we have to decide which priorities get cut. And as much as I'd love for you to get something sporty, with a 200-mile round trip every time you drive to work, I think fuel efficiency, practicality, and reliability should probably win out over being fun to drive in the mountains. This 2020 Toyota Highlander Platinum Hybrid would probably be the most comfortable and reliable, but I don't know about the gear you come home with. If the practicality of having a truck bed is more important than passenger space, take a look at this 2022 Ford F-150 Lariat Hybrid.

The F-150 is rated at 23 mpg combined, which means it will cost a lot more to run than the Highlander, but it's still a hybrid that will get better mileage than a non-hybrid, and with your drive, I'm not sure an F-150 Lightning is the better option. It isn't ideal, but then again, neither is driving 100 miles each way to get to work. Are you sure you couldn't just move closer to work? The F-150 Hybrid would still be a good choice, but come on, man. Don't you want a dozen hours of your life back every week?

Hey David, I know the wildfires in the Pacific Northwest were gnarly this year, so first I'd like to say thank you for doing what you do. Now, as a reward, I think I found the perfect car to safely get you to where you need to go while offering exceptional efficiency and a surprising amount of fun. Don't laugh, but it's a 2023 Toyota Prius AWD listed for sale in Auburn, WA for $28,000.

The fifth-generation Toyota Prius marks the first time that the words "handsome" and "fun" have ever been used when describing what it's like to look at and drive a Prius, with no sarcasm involved. Its 196 horsepower and 139 lb-ft of torque are more than enough to whisk this efficient and sleek hatchback from 0-to-60 in about 7 seconds, so it will offer you a zippy chariot for your 100-mile one-way mountain road commute. Though it's no pickup truck, it is a hugely versatile hatchback that holds around 50 cubic feet of cargo with the rear seats folded, or about 20 with the back seats in place. Beyond those stats, it's powered by a dependable Toyota hybrid drivetrain, so it should offer you reliable, fun, and efficient commuting for hundreds of thousands of miles.

If you need more space, you could easily find a fourth-generation Prius AWD in your price range which offers a bit more cargo space, but that comes at the cost of the spunky drivetrain and sleek styling, but I think it would still be a great fit for your unique needs. Hope this helps!

David. My man. My friend. You're a pillar of the community, a lifesaver, a genuine hero. The kind of public servant that NWA doesn't write songs about. Despite all that, my esteemed coworkers want to put you in anonymous vehicles that barely fit your needs. A bees-forks? A Prius? C'mon now. You deserve something truly deserving of your standing as a firefighter: A bright red Chevy Silverado.

You mentioned a desire for six seats, which this Silverado alone meets — it's got a bench up front, so you can fit five other firefighters along with you. The bed will more than fit all your gear or hardware store runs, and it won't force you to smell it all inside the passenger compartment the way an SUV would. Sure, the truck may not be the most fuel efficient option ever built, but I'd argue it is still fun in its own way. Then again, I'm becoming pickup-brained recently, so take anything I say with a grain of salt.

This Silverado is available in Washington within your budget, with your desired four-wheel-drive and two-bench layout, and all wrapped up in firefighter red. Throw some emergency lights on it, and you won't even need decals to let people know what's going on: A firefighter is coming through, en route to save the day.
