#5739. Managing Metastases in Advanced Prostate Cancer

— Beyond Diagnosis continues with Christopher Wee on radiation therapy and multidisciplinary care

Developed in partnership with the Our Partner

In "Beyond Diagnosis: Metastatic Castration-Sensitive Prostate Cancer," Cleveland Clinic oncologist Christopher Wee, MD, and host John Mangels discuss how clinicians can guide patients through the growing complexities of treatment for metastatic disease.

Each installment of this series explores key moments in patient care, including building trust, navigating evolving therapies, aligning treatment goals, and supporting shared decision-making.

In this fourth episode, Wee discusses the role of radiation in managing metastatic disease, strategies for treating bone metastases and preventing skeletal complications, and the importance of multidisciplinary care in balancing disease control with quality of life.

The following is a transcript of their remarks:

Mangels: Welcome to "Beyond Diagnosis," where we talk with doctors about treatment decisions and communicating with patients. I'm your host, John Mangels.

Treatment of metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer has changed significantly in the last decade. Those changes are creating new opportunities and new complexities for both physicians and patients. How do clinicians choose among expanded treatment options? How do they navigate decisions involving efficacy and risk, quality of life, and patient preferences?

We'll explore those issues and more with our guest, Dr. Christopher Wee. Dr. Wee is a physician in Cleveland Clinic's genitourinary medical oncology program. A large part of his practice involves patients with prostate cancer. Dr. Wee, thanks so much for joining us today.

Mangels: Metastatic disease involves more complexities and more complications potentially than localized prostate cancer. Is your approach to treat metastases individually? Do you try and control them systemically? What's your approach on that?

Wee: Historically, metastatic disease has been a systemic therapy situation, because the spots that you can see on imaging likely underrepresent the true burden of disease. There could be micrometastases elsewhere. And so that's why we don't go and necessarily go after each individual metastasis.

However, there's a caveat, and this is an evolving science. Radiation is becoming an integral part in certain situations. So if someone were to have low-volume de novo metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, there is a survival benefit per the STAMPEDE trial to do prostate-directed radiotherapy. Sometimes we'll even consider metastasis-directed therapy in those situations. And then if something were to become oligoprogressive to castrate-resistant, so let's say someone has castration-sensitive prostate cancer, metastatic, and the PSA [prostate-specific antigen] starts rising, but there's only one or two spots that are really lighting up on a repeat PET, there are emerging data suggesting that radiation or often SBRT [stereotactic body radiotherapy] can be a benefit to that patient because then if they can get control, they don't have to necessarily switch treatment.

So this is evolving science. I think this is where it's very important to have a multidisciplinary team evaluate these situations, but systemic therapy is still the backbone of treatment of metastatic disease.

Mangels: We've talked a lot already about patient communication. When patients learn that their prostate cancer has spread to their bones or say an organ like the liver, that's bound to be frightening to them. How do you help them understand what those findings mean without completely eradicating hope?

Wee: I think it's frightening because of the uncertainty, and I wish I could sometimes give more certainty to patients like this. Most patients want an honest answer. They don't want sugarcoating. So I'll ask a patient, "Do you mind if I'm upfront with you?" Vast majority of the time they want to know. This is generally considered, in historically speaking, not a curable situation, but some patients can live for years, many years. I don't know at this point. Our goal is to try to give you the best outcome possible, and we do this with these treatments and we go from there.

If patients start asking more specifically about life expectancies, again, at the time of metastatic diagnosis, the median overall survival is years. So it's really hard to predict at that point what this is going to look like.

Mangels: And that's so important to emphasize that incurable doesn't mean untreatable.

Mangels: And then I'm guessing the discussion about patient treatment goals, quality of life, all the things we've talked about before becomes even more important.

So bones are by far the most common site of metastasis in prostate cancer. Beyond controlling the cancer itself, what are your priorities when you're treating a patient with skeletal metastases? Are you looking at managing pain? Are you looking at trying to prevent fractures?

Wee: So in castration-sensitive disease, the primary treatment is actually just using systemic therapy, ADT [androgen deprivation therapy] plus ARPI [androgen receptor pathway inhibitor], plus/minus chemo. The role of a bone-modifying agent such as a bisphosphonate like zoledronic acid [Reclast] or RANKL ligand like denosumab [Prolia] is reserved primarily for patients who have osteoporosis. So a bone scan would be helpful, bone density scan. And if someone has osteoporosis, that should be treated appropriately.

If a patient progresses to castration-resistant disease, there is an indication to give a bone-modifying agent to prevent a skeletal-related metastasis. So that's where the conversation comes into even if a patient doesn't have osteoporosis, if they have osseous metastases, there should be consideration to be giving a bone-modifying agent in castration-resistant disease. If there's a symptomatic spot that's causing a lot of trouble, that's a great time to also consider palliative radiation.

Mangels: Let's talk about radiation. When do you bring in radiation oncology and is the goal of the radiation to treat the tumor or to treat the pain or something else?

Wee: In metastatic prostate cancer, there's generally a few reasons. One, as we discussed previously, in de novo low-volume metastatic disease, primary prostatic radiation should be considered due to an overall survival benefit in STAMPEDE trial, but then also palliative radiation to specific spots if they're painful and metastasis-directed therapy.

So this is where the gray area comes in. So let's say someone has low-volume metastatic disease, just a couple of bone spots per se -- and we're getting this more often now that we have PSMA [prostate-specific membrane antigen] PET -- or a couple lymph nodes only. We had talked about previously how the standard of care metastatic disease is indefinite ADT, but what if you were able to zap all the spots of disease with radiation? Could you give a defined course of treatment to give a treatment-free interval? It's unclear the optimal duration and everything, but it's something we talk about with patients.

And anecdotally, some of these patients can get prolonged disease-free intervals where they don't have to be on treatment necessarily. And so that's something where it's shared decision-making with the patient.

Mangels: Are there particular patterns of metastatic spread or symptomatology or lab results, clinical findings that make you think, "Wow, I really need to think about whether this approach with this patient needs to change or not"?

Wee: I think there are two reasons why we would want to change. If one, the treatment regimen we're not doing is not working, or two, if it is not having manageable toxicity. Those are two reasons to change treatment.

Sometimes, this is not the most common situation, but sometimes despite the PSA being low, a patient could be clinically doing worse. They may be having more fatigue, more weight loss. That should be a red flag. At that time, usually I would re-image with conventional imaging if the PSA is low, because what you worry about in those situations is could this be differentiating into another process such as a neuroendocrine differentiation of prostate cancer or small cell neuroendocrine? And that's a lot more aggressive, at which point it needs to be managed differently with a lot more aggressive therapy sometimes.

Mangels: We talked a couple of seconds ago about bringing radiation oncology in, but that sort of opens the door to the importance of multidisciplinary care in these patients. Let's talk about that. You've got orthopedic oncology, I'm guessing, pain management, palliative care, rehab. Talk about how you coordinate all of those and involve all those and why they're important to be involved.

Wee: Absolutely. So radiation oncology is probably the most common one we work with, obviously. Palliative medicine with the symptom support, especially if there's pain involved because we can really improve patients' quality of life and oftentimes extend survival if we have good palliative care.

We're increasingly using our colleagues in nuclear medicine, both from a diagnostic standpoint with the PSMA PET scans as well as therapeutics with radioligand therapy. So this is one of the exciting parts of being a medical oncologist is the team-sport nature of this and how we can all work together to try to do what's best for the patient.

Mangels: Thanks so much for your insights, Dr. Wee. And thank you for joining us on Beyond Diagnosis, where we explore not just what physicians know, but how to effectively and compassionately share that knowledge with patients. See you next time.

#5738. Color Health launches collabs with NCI-designated cancer centers to streamline intake

Color Health launches collabs with NCI-designated cancer centers to streamline intake" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Color Health, a virtual oncologist-led cancer clinic, has announced formal clinical collaborations with 10 National Cancer Institute-designated cancer centers.

Color and collaborating cancer centers aim to streamline time to treatment through coordinated workup (like imaging and labs) and records preparation, as well as custom intake workflows. These elements help ensure a timely start to care when weeks can be the difference between life or death, executives say. Additional partners will be announced in the coming months.

“Speed to diagnosis, speed to treatment initiation, is one of the single biggest determinants of outcomes in cancer," Caroline Savello, president of Color, told Fierce Healthcare. “Where can we make sure that there is the right clinical coordination, the right navigation coordination happening so that things can happen swiftly through the right processes."

Cancer is among the top drivers of healthcare costs and mortality. Because of its complex and variable nature, the quality and timeliness of care are the best ways to improve outcomes and manage costs. That means less duplicate testing, fewer treatment changes later and fewer avoidable ED visits and hospitalizations.

Among the collaborating centers are City of Hope-Los Angeles, Memorial Sloan Kettering, Moffitt Cancer Center, Mount Sinai, Stanford Medicine Cancer Center, UC Davis Comprehensive Cancer Center and UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center. National Cancer Institute (NCI)-designated cancer centers go through a robust evaluation for meeting quality, safety and access standards.

When care at a specific center is determined to be a good fit for a patient, Color coordinates directly to match patients with the right team, completes the clinical workup, reviews medical records and completes authorizations to each center’s specifications. First-appointment targets for most patients are set at seven days or fewer for oncology referrals placed by Color Medical. Additionally, Color verifies insurance coverage to ensure the referral is in-network. Occasionally, Color works with payers or centers on single-case agreements if something is otherwise out of network.

“Color is, above all, a very patient-centered company. When an individual faces a cancer diagnosis for the first time, Color helps to provide the information and navigation to top cancer centers. Their process balances technology with a human touch,” Karen Lu, M.D., physician in chief at Moffitt Cancer Center, told Fierce Healthcare over email.

For any patient issues, Color clinicians escalate to the collaborating centers. Patients also get ongoing wraparound support from Color during and after treatment, including nutrition, mental health, palliative and survivorship care. Additionally, Color will collaborate with the centers to identify any potential clinical trial candidates, gather the needed information and support institution-led eligibility assessment and enrollment.

UCSF Health has already worked with Color for years, so the latest collaboration is an expansion of the partnership.

“[Screening or diagnosis] can be incredibly stressful moments, and navigating a complex healthcare system should not add to that burden,” Laurel Bray-Hanin, VP at UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center, told Fierce Healthcare in emailed comments. “This partnership allows us to connect Color's cancer screening and care coordination efforts directly with UCSF Health's expert patient navigators, who can help patients quickly identify and schedule the appropriate next steps.”

Color “expanded dramatically” this year, per Savello, teaming up with Independence Blue Cross and planning to serve millions more new lives in the new year through employers. Those employers continue to be laser-focused on oncology, per Savello, and are asking Color to set up partnerships with cancer centers in their regions.

“They’re all seeing, obviously, rate increases," she said. "The disease space and the market is very active."

Color partners with local providers to clinically manage all patients through its oncologist-led care team. Its virtual cancer clinic is a national center of excellence certified by the American Society of Clinical Oncology, meaning it meets rigorous standards and is subject to annual audits and reviews. The company, which started working in the cancer space in 2023, says its patients see 66% faster diagnosis and a 77% increase in screening adherence. It also claims to save $62,000 per patient in treatment and closes over three-quarters of costly care gaps.

“Cancer care isn't always a straightforward path. Sometimes, patients need answers about a possible diagnosis, and other times, they need a fresh perspective or access to new treatment options,” Bray-Hanin at UCSF said. “We want patients to feel that someone is looking out for them, helping them understand their options, and connecting them with the expertise and care they need. That commitment to providing compassionate, coordinated care is what makes this partnership so meaningful to us.”

#5737. Hims & Hers reports $890.4M Q3 revenue, tightens 2026 outlook

Hims & Hers reports $890.4M Q3 revenue, tightens 2026 outlook" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Digital health and wellness company Hims & Hers tightened its full-year 2026 revenue outlook after missing Wall Street analysts’ revenue and earnings estimates.

Andrew Dudum, co-founder, chairperson and CEO, pointed investors toward the increasing scale of Hims & Hers' pharmacy and lab infrastructure. That growth is driving efficiencies for the company, as is its artificial intelligence-native experience, he said.

“That infrastructure positions us to launch treatments of increasing complexity, including testosterone replacement therapy this quarter and our Peptides Plus offering later this month,” Dudum said.

Peptides have been a focus for the company as of late, with Dudum telling investors last quarter it plans to offer already-permitted peptides, like sermorelin and NAD+.

Dudum said that Hims & Hers’ long-term strategy focuses on “three critical commitments:” being a leader in metabolic health domestically and globally, leading major markets globally and being "at the forefront of category expansion.”

“Each of these reinforces the other, and together they describe how Hims & Hers becomes the global destination for consumer health,” he said. “We are investing aggressively against all three because this opportunity is growing quickly, and we believe it will become more valuable every quarter.”

The company reported $890.4 million in revenue in Q3, up 49% compared to revenue of $599 million the year prior, according to financial results published Monday. Net loss was $33 million, compared to $15.8 million in profit for the same quarter a year ago.

Chief Financial Officer Yemi Okupe said that revenue excluded $18 million from the “scaling of membership revenue” in the company’s weight loss offering but will be recognized in the fourth quarter.

“This revenue deferral has no impact on free cash flow generation,” Okupe noted.

Adjusted EBITDA was $82.4 million compared to $78.4 million the year prior.

Ethan Feller, stock strategist at Zacks Investment Research, told Fierce Healthcare the company’s revenue was “roughly what Wall Street expected,” adding that U.S. “growth sped up to 21%.”

“But the company lost 14 cents a share against an expected gain of six cents, its third big miss in a row,” Feller said. “It is also keeping less of each sale, as gross margin fell to 57%, down from 74% a year ago, as more of the business shifts to lower-margin brand-name weight-loss drugs.”

Feller added that the company’s “growth story is still a real long-term tailwind.”

“Demand for weight-loss drugs is strong, and having both Novo and Lilly on the platform helps,” Feller said. “But as long as margins keep shrinking, the stock will likely stay under pressure until either the price falls to a level that reflects the lower margins or the company shows it can turn a steady profit.”

As a result, Hims & Hers tightened its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to a range of $3.13 billion to $3.15 billion and reduced its adjusted EBITDA guidance to a range of $257 million to $277 million.

“This is a reflection of the more aggressive strategic pricing and marketing actions that we expect to take in the U.K. and Germany, and the weight loss membership deferral noted above,” Okupe said.

The earnings report comes on the heels of an announcement that the company struck a deal with Eli Lilly to offer its branded obesity treatments directly through the Hims & Hers platform. The drugs were previously only available to patients if they left the site and went to Lilly's direct-to-consumer platform, LillyDirect.

“Nearly 3 million people across four continents rely on us to access care,” Dudum said. “That trust has made us a valuable partner to global pharmaceutical leaders like Novo and Lilly, and positions us to keep bringing the most innovative treatments to our customers as they come to market.”

Dudum added that the company is planning to launch “flexible multi-month subscriptions” across its assortment to make it easier for customers to address health goals.

“We will continue to prioritize partnerships across the industry, with the goal that whenever an innovative therapy reaches the market, our customers can access it here,” Dudum said. “That assortment will sit alongside an AI-native experience that will soon be available to nearly every weight loss customer on our platform.”

For example, treating perimenopause symptoms remains a challenge due to a lack of standardized diagnostics. “What we’re trying to do is really educate women and make it a safe place for women to come and talk about what they’re experiencing, and get high quality clinical care, so they don’t have to suffer through it,” Kubal said.

The DTC business, which launched six months ago, “is seeing really great traction from consumers,” per Kubal. It has grown by 55% a month, on average, in terms of subscriptions. In October, its GLP-1 program grew 80% from the prior month. While government payers are part of the discussion, going in-network with them is not on Maven's immediate roadmap, Kubal said.

#5734. Another Promising Study on Statins in Compensated Cirrhosis

— There are no approved treatments to prevent hepatic decompensation

Statin initiation among adults with compensated cirrhosis was associated with a lower risk of hepatic decompensation and lower overall mortality, according to a large observational study.

Among over 18,000 patients, the cumulative incidence of hepatic decompensation was 18.2% for those who took statins versus 22.7% for those who didn't take statins (adjusted subhazard ratio [aSHR] 0.86, 95% CI 0.78-0.96, P=0.008), reported Monica Tincopa, MD, of the University of California San Diego, at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases annual meeting in Denver.

The cumulative incidence of overall mortality was 14.6% for statin users compared with 21.2% for non-users (aSHR 0.77, 95% CI 0.68-0.87, P<0.001).

Over 5 years, the number needed to treat to prevent one episode of decompensation was 25, a number that dropped to 21 over 8 years.

"Decompensation really is the turning point in cirrhosis," Tincopa said. Without approved treatments to prevent decompensation, "current options are really limited to treating the underlying causes of liver disease."

Statins offer potential anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic benefits in cirrhosis, as well as reductions in hepatic portal vein pressure. However, research on statins and decompensation prevention has delivered "highly conflicting" results, Tincopa noted.

Other observational studies have suggested that statin use is associated with lower risks of decompensation and death, including research in veterans with hepatitis C-related compensated cirrhosis. But randomized trials have shown unfavorable results. Ongoing studies such as the phase III SACRED trial of simvastatin in patients with high-risk compensated cirrhosis could bring greater clarity.

The current study included adults with cirrhosis and no prior hepatic decompensation, as determined by ICD-10 codes. Patients with liver transplant or HIV were excluded. The investigators analyzed electronic health record data from the University of California Health Data Warehouse on patients seen at affiliated health facilities from 2012 to 2026.

Statin users and non-users had to have no statin in the 90 days after a cirrhosis diagnosis. Statin users received a prescription after that 90-day lead-in period and had a 90-day qualifying window in which they had no decompensations or deaths. Follow-up for both groups began at 180 days after a cirrhosis diagnosis.

Median age at cirrhosis diagnosis was 58 years, 44% of patients were women, and 51% were white. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) was the cause of cirrhosis in 73.7% of statin users and 59% of non-users, and the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score was at least 10 in 2.9% of statin users and 9.4% of non-users. Coronary artery disease was present in 17.9% of statin patients and 3.5% of those who didn't take statins.

The median duration of statin exposure was about 2.6 years, and 75% of statins taken were lipophilic. Median follow-up time was 7.9 years after cirrhosis diagnosis.

First decompensation events were lower in statin users versus non-users, including ascites (12.7% vs 17.1%, respectively), hepatic encephalopathy (4.8% vs 6.5%), variceal bleeding (1.4% vs 2.1%), hepatorenal syndrome (0.3% vs 0.7%), and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (0.2% vs 0.6%).

Limitations included potential residual confounding and the use of ICD-10 codes to determine cirrhosis and outcomes. The study also didn't assess statin doses or formulations.

#5731. Advances and Unmet Needs in Pediatric Sickle Cell Disease

— It's better care that has led to better survival, not new treatment options

As the 1970s came to a close, sickle cell disease (SCD) remained largely a pediatric condition because few children born in the U.S. with the condition survived to adulthood. Today, about 95% of children born with SCD in developed nations survive to adulthood. Median life expectancy in the U.S. has reached 60 years, meaning half of all patients live to that age, as compared with less than 40% just 10 years ago.

The dramatic improvement in survival evolved from an amalgamation of factors including universal screening of newborns, prophylactic penicillin to prevent bacterial infections, immunization against Haemophilus influenzae and Streptococcus pneumoniae, and broader and better-informed use of FDA-approved therapies for SCD. A recent multi-article review covered some of the key developments, as well as ongoing challenges and unmet needs.

Ironically, a clinical trial that did not meet its primary endpoint has profoundly influenced management of SCD. The randomized, placebo-controlled BABY HUG trial failed to show that hydroxyurea reduced the risk of kidney and spleen damage by 50% in very young children with SCD. Nonetheless, the trial showed that patients randomized to hydroxyurea had significantly fewer SCD-associated clinical events, including pain, dactylitis, acute chest syndrome, blood transfusion, and hospitalization. Investigators concluded that hydroxyurea "can now be considered for all very young children with sickle cell anemia."

BABY HUG was a landmark clinical trial because of the history of hydroxyurea, which was initially approved only for adults with SCD who met specific high-risk criteria. Published more than a decade ago, the trial established clinical principles that remain highly relevant today for children with SCD.

"[BABY HUG] gave us the evidence that hydroxyurea can be used as prevention, so before kids start having all these complications," Allison King, MD, MPH, PhD, of Washington University in St. Louis, told MedPage Today. "BABY HUG was really helpful because instead of being so reactive, the practice could be very proactive in pediatrics."

A recent analysis of more than 2,000 children with sickle cell anemia treated with hydroxyurea established long-term safety and efficacy. Children followed for as long as 8 years had significantly fewer and briefer hospitalizations, and laboratory data showed sustained improvement in hemoglobin in patients with good treatment adherence.

The Silent Cerebral Infarct Transfusion trial, published more than a decade ago, also had a transformative impact on SCD management. The results, in 200 children with sickle cell anemia, showed that regular blood transfusions significantly reduced the risk of silent cerebral infarction, which can have more subtle neurologic effects as compared with a stroke.

"A lot of our kids, and adults, have cognitive deficits, which are kind of like invisible disabilities because [the patients] can be quite verbal but have significant attention problems, processing speed, executive function that limit their ability to progress in their daily activities," said King. "Also, silent infarcts are a high risk for having overt strokes. Now it's an evidence-based guideline that we should be screening, as well as responding and transfusing, to prevent the progression."

Fast forward a decade and gene therapy became the next transformative clinical development in SCD, offering the potential for cure. Unfortunately, other therapeutic options for SCD have remained limited throughout the decade. One of the approved drugs, voxelotor (Oxbryta), was withdrawn from the market after post-approval data analysis and real-world clinical experience showed the benefits no longer outweighed the risks. Concern has arisen about the future status of another approved agent, crizanlizumab (Adakveo), which lost its conditional European marketing approval. Additionally, the drug failed to outperform placebo for reducing episodes of vaso-occlusive crisis in a recent phase III trial.

Moreover, cost and access remain major obstacles to expansion of gene therapy as a treatment option. In 2025, fewer than 200 patients worldwide received the two gene therapies, which come with a hefty price tag of $2-$3 million. Additionally, the process for screening and preparing patients for gene therapy can be "laborious" for many families, said King.

Despite the advances, more and more effective therapies are an ongoing need for patients with SCD, said Ofelia Alvarez, MD, of the University of Miami Health System.

"There is still a lot to do," she told MedPage Today. "The most widely used medication, hydroxyurea, does not work for all children with sickle cell anemia. Some patients do not respond. They continue to have low hemoglobin despite the treatment. We need new therapies to improve anemia, to decrease complications. They are always in need."

Better transitional care also has contributed to better survival in SCD. However, the quality of care and the ability to provide good transitional care vary greatly. Transition involves much more than handing off a patient from pediatric care to adult care, said Alvarez. Most young patients need to be educated about the disease itself, what medications are available and how they are used, and how to make appointments. Some need to learn about practical issues, such as budgeting, transportation, and learning to live independently.

"Here at the University of Miami, we have a very robust program that is co-created with patients and explained to the parents," said Alvarez. "After the transition, we follow up with the patients to see how they feel about the process and whether they have become integrated into the [adult] practice... . I personally don't have a lot of problems because I work very closely with the adult providers."

In some settings and circumstances, transition into adult care can be complicated and anything but a smooth process. The age at transition varies from practice to practice, but 18 is a common age. King, who specializes in caring for children, has expanded her patient age range up to 26. She described a 23-year-old patient whose circumstances are not rare in the SCD community.

"He has been intermittently homeless for 2 years," said King. "In his words, he 'couch surfs.' He doesn't have a stable place to live. He's not sure where he's getting his food. His meds are always being stolen, so he's frequently in the hospital for pain."

The case also illustrates the problem with using pain as a patient-reported endpoint for judging treatment efficacy, which has been a historical standard for the FDA.

"Pain is so multifactorial," said King. "It could be just sickling, and I'm not trying to minimize that, but it could be very biologically driven, but often, particularly in older teens and adults, psychosocial factors really are big drivers. That makes it difficult to tease out what's really driving a patient's pain."

Finding the origin of a patient's pain has been complicated by the fact that "for the last 20 years, we were sort of crawling our way out of the opioid crisis," said Jeffrey Glassberg, MD, of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City.

"When I was in med school, we were taught that there was no danger to opioids," Glassberg told MedPage Today. "If you're treating pain, no harm could come to the patient. Today, I think most people who treat a lot of sickle cell patients would agree: Opioids cause pain. Full stop."

"We have noted that the more opioids that we were giving over the last couple of decades, the more pain our patients would experience, and that pain is non-vaso-occlusive," he continued. "Our latest research is really finding that patients feel that the pain is identical to vaso-occlusive crisis ... The more opioids you give, the more pain that patients will experience that's non-vaso-occlusive, but feels the same."

A number of candidate drugs for SCD have failed to pass muster with the FDA because they did not show a reduction in vaso-occlusive crises. Moving away from that as an endpoint for efficacy and toward a more objective endpoint -- such as organ damage -- might increase the likelihood of more drug approvals and more treatment options for patients, said Glassberg.

#5729. Scientists discover surprising heart benefits of eating avocado and mango every day

Eating mango and avocado every day could offer unexpected benefits for heart health, according to new research. In a study lasting just eight weeks, adults with prediabetes who regularly ate both fruits experienced improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure, without gaining weight or consuming more calories.

The findings could be especially relevant to the one in three (98 million) Americans with prediabetes, a condition in which blood sugar levels are elevated but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, the research suggests that incorporating these two nutrient-rich fruits into everyday meals may help support cardiovascular health.

Researchers at Illinois Institute of Technology (Illinois Tech) investigated the effects of an Avocado-Mango (AM) diet that included one medium Hass avocado and one cup of fresh mango each day. Participants followed this eating plan for eight weeks, while a comparison group consumed a similar diet in which the fruits were replaced with carbohydrate-based foods containing equivalent calories.

The results revealed notable differences between the groups, particularly in how well their blood vessels functioned and how their blood pressure changed over time.

One of the clearest improvements involved the ability of blood vessels to expand as blood flows through them. This flexibility helps maintain healthy circulation and is an important indicator of cardiovascular health.

To evaluate this response, researchers measured flow-mediated dilation (FMD), a commonly used test of endothelial function (blood vessel health). The endothelium is the thin layer of cells lining the inside of blood vessels, where it helps regulate circulation and the widening and narrowing of arteries.

Among participants eating avocado and mango, the measurement increased significantly to 6.7%. In contrast, it declined to 4.6% in the control group. The difference suggests that regularly consuming these fruits may help blood vessels function more effectively.

Blood pressure measurements also showed encouraging changes, especially among male participants. Men in the control group experienced an average increase of 5 points (mmHg) in central blood pressure, while those consuming avocado and mango saw a reduction of approximately 1.9 points.

Diastolic blood pressure, the lower number in a blood pressure reading, reflects the pressure inside arteries when the heart relaxes between beats. Maintaining healthy levels is important because elevated blood pressure can place additional strain on the cardiovascular system. Researchers noted that the differences observed in the study could be clinically meaningful if they persist over time.

Importantly, the cardiovascular improvements occurred without significant changes in participants' body weight or total calorie consumption. This suggests that the nutritional quality of the foods people eat may influence heart health even when their weight remains stable.

“This research reinforces the power of food-first strategies to help reduce cardiovascular disease risk, particularly in vulnerable populations like those with prediabetes,” said Britt Burton-Freeman, PhD, Principal Investigator and Professor at Illinois Tech. “It’s an encouraging message: small, nutrient-dense additions—like incorporating avocado and mango into meals and snacks—may support heart health without the need for strict rules or major dietary overhauls.”

Beyond the improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure, participants eating mango and avocado consumed more fiber, vitamin C, and monounsaturated fat. These nutrients are associated with cardiovascular wellness and may help explain some of the observed benefits.

Researchers also identified improvements in certain indicators of kidney health, including estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), a measurement used to assess how effectively the kidneys filter waste from the blood.

However, the fruits did not produce significant improvements in every health measurement. Cholesterol levels, blood sugar, and markers of inflammation remained largely unchanged compared with the control group.

Together, the results suggest that regularly including nutrient-rich fruits in the diet could be a practical way to support cardiovascular health, particularly for people with prediabetes who face an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

Although mango and avocado have very different flavors and nutritional profiles, they provide complementary nutrients that support several aspects of cardiovascular and metabolic health.

Mango provides dietary fiber (2g/serving, 7% DV, Mango serving size: ¾ cup) and is an excellent source of vitamin C (50% DV). Vitamin C is an antioxidant that helps protect cells from damage, while fiber contributes to healthy digestion and may help with blood sugar regulation, weight management, and cardiovascular wellness.

Avocado offers another combination of potentially beneficial nutrients. It contains fiber (3g/serving, 11% DV, Avocado serving size: 50 g (1/3 of a medium avocado)), which plays a role in managing cholesterol, blood sugar, and body weight.

It also supplies unsaturated fats (6g unsaturated fats), which can support heart health by helping reduce LDL cholesterol, often called bad cholesterol, when they replace less healthy fats in the diet. Additionally, avocado contains potassium (250mg, 6% DV), a mineral involved in regulating blood pressure.

By providing fiber, antioxidants, healthy fats, and potassium, mango and avocado offer a convenient way to increase the nutritional value of everyday meals. However, the study did not establish whether eating the two fruits together provides greater benefits than consuming either fruit separately.

Incorporating these fruits into meals does not require a complicated eating plan. Their contrasting flavors and textures make them useful ingredients in salads, smoothies, and grain bowls.

For example, fresh mango can add sweetness to a savory dish, while avocado contributes a rich, creamy texture. Both can be used in recipes such as Mango Avocado Tuna Ceviche or an Avocado and Mango Topper.

Additional recipes and nutritional information are available at Mango.org and LoveOneToday.com.

The investigation included 82 adults between the ages of 25 and 60 who had prediabetes and were classified as having overweight or obesity (BMI 25–35 kg/m2). All participants were generally healthy, did not smoke, were not following specialized diets, and had no major chronic medical conditions.

Over eight weeks, participants followed calorie-controlled eating plans modeled on typical American dietary patterns. One group ate a medium Hass avocado and a cup of fresh mango daily, while the control group received carbohydrate-based alternatives with comparable calorie content.

To make the comparison as consistent as possible, researchers prepared and supplied meals covering 75% of each participant's estimated daily calorie needs. Participants chose their remaining foods independently, allowing some flexibility while helping the researchers limit differences between the two diets and encourage adherence.

The primary measurement was flow-mediated dilation (FMD), a noninvasive method for assessing how effectively blood vessels respond to increased circulation. Researchers also examined blood pressure, blood sugar, and other metabolic indicators, inflammation, kidney function, and dietary nutrient intake.

Despite the additional fruits, the avocado and mango group did not experience significant changes in body weight or overall calorie intake. This finding suggests that incorporating nutrient-dense foods into an otherwise balanced diet may improve certain aspects of cardiometabolic health without necessarily contributing to weight gain.

The study had several strengths, including its carefully controlled feeding approach, two parallel comparison groups, and emphasis on whole fruits rather than isolated nutrients or supplements.

However, researchers also acknowledged important limitations. The intervention lasted only eight weeks, so it remains unclear whether the improvements would persist over months or years. The participants also represented a relatively narrow population of adults with prediabetes and overweight or obesity, meaning the findings may not apply equally to people with different health conditions or dietary habits.

The research measured cardiovascular risk indicators rather than long-term outcomes such as heart attacks or strokes. Larger and longer studies will be needed to determine whether the observed changes translate into lasting reductions in cardiovascular disease risk.

Nevertheless, the findings offer an encouraging indication that relatively modest changes in food choices may benefit blood vessel health, even without weight loss or a major dietary overhaul.

This study was supported through an unrestricted grant from the National Mango Board (NMB) and the Hass Avocado Board (HAB). NMB and HAB had no role in the study design or findings.

#5728. All of Us study finds thousands of new genetic variants affecting drug responses

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Anil Oza is a general assignment reporter at STAT focused on the NIH and health equity. You can reach him on Signal at aniloza.16.

A study of nearly 100,000 Americans identified thousands of new variants in a set of genes that influence our responses to prescription drugs, thanks to the inclusion of participants from a more diverse set of ancestries than previous studies of these so-called pharmacogenes.

Using data from the National Institute of Health’s All of Us program, the researchers found that every participant carried at least one variant in the 16 pharmacogenes they studied, and that one in four participants had taken a medication that could be affected by these variants.

The new paper, published Wednesday in Science Translational Medicine, advances efforts to use genetic data to personalize drug treatments, and should make this area of research useful to a broader population.

“This really furthers the emerging evidence of how genetically guided clinical care adds benefit across a diverse population,” said Loren Saulsberry, a health policy researcher who has done work on equity and pharmacogenomics but was not involved in the new paper.

Pharmacogenes can change the way people metabolize drugs such that they need higher or lower doses, face worse or new side effects, or in some cases make drugs entirely ineffective. The variants included in the study affect the functioning of drugs including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, statins, chemotherapy, and the blood thinner Plavix, among others.

“If you have a prior experience with a medicine that did not work for you, or had a side effect, we can’t say it’s absolutely because of genetics, but we are appreciating more and more that people are different, and genetics is one reason that may suggest where there may be differences,” said Philip Empey, who directs the Center for Clinical Pharmaceutical Sciences at the University of Pittsburgh and was the senior author on the paper.

The paper points to the need to give more attention to the role genetics plays in the clinic, Empey added. But there are a number of barriers before these results can make their way into patient care. Many people don’t have their genomes sequenced, physicians may not be aware of how drugs they are prescribing are affected by genetic variants, and there are a constellation of variants that could impact drugs.

The All of Us Research Program has the goal of collecting genetic data from 1 million Americans from diverse backgrounds. That diversity helped identify variants not found in previous work using other genomic databases like the U.K. Biobank.

Part of the concern with new technologies is that they may not be as effective for marginalized populations, but having such a diverse dataset to start with will help limit disparities in outcomes as the findings are translated into clinical use, Saulsberry said.

The potential benefits of All of Us’s data going forward may be affected by funding woes. The program is supported by two sources: the 21st Century Cures Act, enacted in 2016, and yearly appropriations from Congress. That former avenue will dry up in the 2027 fiscal year. Congress is currently operating under a temporary budget, called a continuing resolution, but the program expects to receive $122 million in funding once a budget is finalized, an 80% drop from its peak in 2023.

Those cuts have meant that All of Us has had to be less ambitious in its recruiting of patients, said Joshua Denny, who was CEO of the program until the end of October and is now in a leadership position at the University of Chicago. “The engagement activities, the brick and mortar that we had enrolling at academic medical centers and FQHCs and mobile units. These kinds of things … were cut back dramatically,” he said. The program has also stopped offering participants the ability to see the results of their genetic testing because of funding concerns.

Another area where All of Us has had to temper its aims has been with recruiting children, which it began in 2023. At this point, it has around 5,000 children enrolled in the study but those data are not yet available to researchers, said Sara Van Driest, director of pediatrics for All of Us.

“In order to really enroll children at scale and build a dataset that’s going to fuel the future of precision health, we’re going to need stable funding in the years ahead,” she added. “I should say, increased and stable funding in the years ahead.”

Anil Oza is a general assignment reporter at STAT focused on the NIH and health equity. You can reach him on Signal at aniloza.16.

#5726. Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response

Children who consume more ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may have stronger brain responses to tempting foods, potentially helping explain why these products are associated with weight gain. A new study published in JAMA Network Open found that children who ate more of these foods showed heightened activity in the brain's reward system when looking at pictures of appetizing foods. Those stronger responses were also associated with increases in body fat over the following year.

Ultra-processed foods include many everyday products, such as breakfast cereals, packaged bread, and instant soups. They are manufactured to be appealing, convenient, and able to remain fresh for extended periods. Many contain artificial sweeteners, coloring agents, and other ingredients rarely used in home cooking. These products make up a substantial portion of children's diets, accounting for approximately 67% of the calories consumed by children in the United States.

Previous research has associated ultra-processed food consumption with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. However, scientists are still trying to understand the biological processes that might explain these connections. The new investigation, supported in part by the National Institutes of Health, combined magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), dietary assessments, and measurements of children's body composition to explore whether the brain's response to food could play a role.

"Children's brains are still developing, habits are still forming and food preferences are still being made. It's an important period where the brain is very sensitive to food and the food environment," said the study's senior author, Kathleen A. Page, MD, professor of medicine and pediatrics and co-chief of the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. "We're particularly interested in understanding these processes in children, because we believe that intervening early could make a real difference."

Brain Scans Reveal a Link to Future Weight Gain

To investigate these connections, the research team studied 46 children between the ages of seven and 10 who were enrolled in the ongoing BrainChild study, which examines factors contributing to diabetes and obesity. Every participant had a healthy weight when the research began, giving scientists an opportunity to investigate potential warning signs before excess weight developed.

The brain scans revealed a notable pattern. Children who consumed larger amounts of ultra-processed foods showed greater activity in the dorsal striatum when viewing food pictures. This part of the brain helps regulate reward and motivation, making it particularly relevant to how people respond to desirable foods.

Importantly, children with stronger responses in this brain region also tended to experience greater increases in BMI and body fat percentage over the next year. The findings suggest that heightened sensitivity to food cues may be one factor connecting ultra-processed diets with subsequent weight gain.

How Brain Reward Activity May Influence Body Fat

By the end of the study, children who consumed more ultra-processed foods generally had higher BMI, greater body fat percentage, and larger waist circumference.

The researchers then examined whether differences in brain activity could help account for these associations. When they adjusted their analysis to consider the children's responses in the dorsal striatum, the relationship between ultra-processed food intake and BMI became 31% weaker. The corresponding association with body fat percentage decreased by 44%.

These reductions suggest that the brain's reward response may help explain part of the relationship between ultra-processed food consumption and changes in body composition. Although the results do not demonstrate that these foods directly alter brain function, they provide a possible biological explanation for an association that has been observed in previous research.

"This study goes beyond just understanding that UPFs affect weight gain," Page said. "It actually gives us insight into the neurobiological underpinnings by which these foods may be linked to body composition over time."

The researchers caution that improving children's diets cannot depend entirely on individual families. Ultra-processed products are often inexpensive, widely available, and easy to prepare, making them practical choices for households facing financial or time constraints.

"Changing the food environment to help people access healthier, more minimally processed foods is an important part of the solution," Page said.

There are also important limitations to consider. Because the study was observational, it cannot determine whether eating ultra-processed foods directly causes heightened brain activity or increases in body weight. The findings establish relationships between these factors, but additional research is needed to determine whether one causes another.

Page hopes to address that question in a future intervention study. The proposed research would provide children who regularly consume ultra-processed foods with more minimally processed alternatives. Scientists could then examine whether changing their diets affects how their brains respond to food images and whether any differences are associated with reduced weight gain.

Meanwhile, the BrainChild study will continue tracking participants as they move through puberty and into early adulthood. By monitoring brain development, body composition, dietary patterns, and general health over time, researchers hope to gain a clearer picture of how childhood nutrition may influence long-term health.

The study was led by Page alongside Jasmin M. Alves, Ella Morgan, Brendan Angelo, Kianna Le, and Jared Smith from the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes, Department of Medicine, and Diabetes and Obesity Research Institute at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, University of Southern California. Additional contributors included Kay Jann of the USC Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, University of Southern California, and Ting Chow and Anny H. Xiang of the Department of Research and Evaluation at Kaiser Permanente Southern California in Pasadena, California.

Funding came from an American Diabetes Association Pathway Accelerator Award [1-14-ACE-36] and the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) [R01DK116858, R01DK134079]. Support for the REDCap database used in the research was provided by the Southern California Clinical and Translational Science Institute [NIH UL1TR001855].

#5725. Response to Standard PBC Treatment at 1 Year Linked to Lower Long-Term Risks

— "Response predicts outcomes in real-world care, and nonresponders carry a risk," researcher says

A biochemical response to ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) at 12 months was associated with lower 5-year risks of hepatic decompensation and mortality in patients with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), a propensity-matched landmark cohort study suggested.

Among patients considered to be responders -- defined as an alkaline phosphatase (ALP) level ≤130 U/L and a bilirubin level ≤1.0 mg/dL -- the 5-year cumulative incidence of hepatic decompensation was 10.2% versus 17.8% among nonresponders (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.51-0.70, P<0.001), reported EzzElDien A. Ibrahim, MD, MSc, of the University of Missouri in Columbia, at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases annual meeting in Denver.

In addition, the cumulative incidence of 5-year all-cause mortality was 12.2% among responders versus 16.3% for nonresponders (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65-0.84, P<0.001).

Other clinical outcomes also trended in favor of or significantly favored responders:

"Response predicts outcomes in real-world care, and nonresponders carry a risk," Ibrahim said. "We can check ALP and bilirubin at 1 year on UDCA," and at that point, clinicians should consider "escalating nonresponders without delay."

UDCA is the first-line treatment for PBC, a rare and chronic autoimmune disease of the bile ducts, "and it ... works," Ibrahim noted.

An international cohort study that included 3,902 patients from the Global PBC Study Group database showed that after inverse probability treatment weighting, the 10-year cumulative liver transplant-free survival rate was 79.7% among UDCA-treated patients and 60.7% among untreated patients, with UDCA treatment resulting in a statistically significantly reduced risk of liver transplant or death (HR 0.46, 95% CI 0.40-0.52, P<0.001).

However, 20% to 40% of patients do not respond biochemically to UDCA at 12 months. In 2024, seladelpar (Livdelzi) and elafibranor (Iqirvo) were granted accelerated approval for patients with PBC who either did not respond to UDCA or were intolerant to the treatment.

While a number of criteria such as the PARIS criteria link 12-month response to UDCA to outcomes, Ibrahim said real-world validation in routine care for 5-year clinical endpoints -- such as decompensation and death -- is limited.

This explains "why this study matters," he noted.

For this study, Ibrahim and colleagues used the TriNetX U.S. Research Network that includes data on 147.5 million patients from 112 health systems.

They included matched cohorts of 2,911 patients with PBC. Mean age was 61.3, 87% were women, 77% were white, 34% had a cirrhosis code, 14% had portal hypertension, and mean albumin level was 3.86-3.91 g/dL.

Responders and nonresponders to UDCA were categorized based on propensity score matching of 29 covariates that included demographics, liver and mental health comorbidities, alanine aminotransferase levels, aspartate aminotransferase levels, platelet counts, albumin levels, and international normalized ratio.

Ibrahim acknowledged that the study had a number of limitations, including the fact that PBC was defined by codes and not by a positive anti-mitochondrial antibody test or histology. In addition, there was no access to UDCA dose or adherence data, and there were a limited number of 5-year events for the liver transplant and hepatocellular carcinoma analyses.

#5724. Newly elected doctors and scientists hope to restore trust in science. It won’t be easy

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Nicholas Florko covers trust in science for STAT, aiming to help readers understand the lived experiences of people who distrust science and to probe why that distrust exists and its consequences. Reach him on Signal at nickflorko.44

Last week, doctors and scientists across the country persuaded Americans to vote them into office. Now comes the hard part: Convincing those who didn’t trust them to believe in their mission.

Doctors and public health officials ran pro-vaccine, pro-science campaigns and won over voters even in traditionally conservative areas. Candidates endorsed by the organization 314 Action, which works to elect Democratic doctors and scientists, flipped 10 congressional seats in last week’s election.

“What we saw in the results is that when these scientists really leaned into their scientific and medical backgrounds, that only provided their potential constituents with more trust,” said Shaughnessy Naughton, the founder of 314 Action. “They are looked at as truth tellers and that really is what people want.”

But the midterm results also clearly demonstrate that Americans remain deeply divided on core scientific issues, with some communities remaining distrustful of the cornerstones of public health policy.

South Carolina elected a pediatrician, Annie Andrews, as the first Democrat to represent the state in the Senate since 2005, but it also voted for 18 officials who publicly pledged to remove Covid vaccines from the market, according to the anti-vaccine advocacy group Americans for Health Freedom.

Across the nation, more than 120 lawmakers publicly opposed to Covid shots were elected to office, according to Americans for Health Freedom. Anti-vaccine sentiment in statehouses has the potential to reshape vaccine policy. Last year, several states passed into law bills that vaccine advocates say would curb vaccine distribution and uptake.

On a statewide level, not all elections went pro-science either. While much attention has been paid to Ohio’s decision to elect Democrat Amy Acton, who led the state’s Covid response, as its next governor, Florida’s next governor will be Byron Donalds, who has said removing all state vaccine requirements would be a “step in the right direction.” Donalds’ challenger, David Jolly, publicly pledged to “bring back science, data, math, vaccines, and public health.”

Brian Castrucci, a Republican who leads the de Beaumont Foundation, which promotes public health, told STAT newly elected public health experts must now answer the question: Why should I trust you?

“We can answer that question, but it’s not going to be by telling people they’re wrong,” Castrucci said.

The newly elected class of doctors and scientists seem particularly well suited to make the case for why their advice on topics like infectious disease should be heeded, several public health experts said. Andrews, for example, has taken to social media to encourage vaccination and has encouraged other doctors to do the same. Castrucci called El-Sayed “one of the best communicators I have ever met in my career .”

“Having leaders who can really communicate how devastating these policies have been and the consequences, I think, is really, really helpful,” said Jeanne Marrazzo, CEO of the Infectious Disease Society of America.

Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat who will represent Michigan in the Senate, has written about the need to improve communication with those who are skeptical of science. “Yelling ‘trust the science!’ at someone who’s afraid of vaccinating does little to allay their underlying fear. Rather, it gives them more reason not to trust  — you, the vaccine, ‘the science,’” he wrote in a column for the Detroit Metro Times in 2024.

In an interview with STAT Wednesday, he argued that “the root cause of the distrust in public health has less to do with distrust in science and a lot more to do with distrust with greed.”

El-Sayed said he hopes to build trust through his efforts to “reinvigorate a movement for public health that is willing to stand up to the power of big corporations,” and to “show the grifters for who they are.”

El-Sayed has made no secret of his desire to use his new power to investigate the actions of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., telling STAT prior to the election that he is eager to “grill” the secretary.

Democrat Richard Pan, a physician elected to represent Sacramento County, Calif., in the House of Representatives, told STAT that while building back trust is going to be difficult, the first step is to “expose the corruption and bad decision-making” of the current administration.

“This administration and RFK Jr. and the people who he has appointed … have all undermined the idea that you can actually trust the federal government,” he said.

Following the election, several Democratic lawmakers, including Patty Murray, vice chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, renewed calls for Kennedy to step down or be fired. A number of Democratic lawmakers have been calling for Kennedy’s ouster for more than a year, citing a lack of confidence in his ability to “carry out the duties of his office.”

Democrats hope gaining the power to subpoena Trump administration officials will allow them to make headway on the investigations they launched when they were in the minority.

“We’ve not even really been able to get information out of RFK and the department,” Rep. Lauren Underwood (D-Ill.), co-chair of the House Democratic Policy and Communications Committee, told STAT. The Democratic majority in Congress means “we’re going to be able to do really vigorous oversight, help people understand how we are fighting for them, and then giving them accurate information,” she added.

While much of the work of congressional investigations occurs behind closed doors through document requests, subpoenas, and sworn depositions, it could also mean Kennedy is brought before congressional committees now under Democratic control, to answer for various policy decisions under oath. Some lawmakers are indicating he will be a frequent guest on Capitol Hill.

“Unless RFK Jr. is interested in spending the next two years in front of Congressional committees, he should go ahead and resign now,” Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) tweeted after the election. Andrews has called Kennedy her “professional archnemesis for decades.”

El-Sayed acknowledged Wednesday that perhaps too much focus is on Kennedy himself, rather than his decisions. “Any investigation that we’re doing is about trying to correct the problems and address the flaws and the faults, rather than trying to achieve any sort of retribution,” El-Sayed said.

Several other Democratic lawmakers agreed that their intention in the next Congress will not be to weaponize or politicize science, but to restore faith in the existing system.

“Democrats will work to restore our scientific infrastructure and integrity and end this administration’s politicization of science,” Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) said in a statement. There is also hope among some Democrats that these inquiries can be bipartisan. Republicans are “not all happy with what’s happened to the science programs,” said Zoe Lofgren (D-Calif.), who wants to lead the House Science Committee.

Still, there could be risks in aggressively investigating Kennedy. Research suggests that  political fights over vaccines can be a net negative for vaccine acceptance. A 2015 paper found that statehouse debates over the HPV vaccine, for example, resulted in “decreases in support for HPV vaccine requirements, state immunization programs, and confidence in doctors and in government.”

It’s an open question whether engaging in a political debate with Kennedy will serve to  deepen skepticism of public health measures, or whether polarization over vaccines has already hit a ceiling, said Sarah Gollust, a professor at the University of Minnesota School of Public Health.

“I’m not sure it can get worse in terms of how politically charged the vaccine issue has been since Covid-19,” said Gollust, one of the 2015 paper’s authors. “We’ve never been here before. We are in very new territory.”

When asked about this potential risk, Pan downplayed the number of ardent Kennedy supporters who currently exist and would be further emboldened by Democrats’ fights with the HHS secretary. “There’s only a very small number of people who really believe in RFK Jr.,” Pan said.

Exactly how true that is remains up for debate. Several candidates endorsed by Kennedy’s MAHA movement did lose elections last week. And Kennedy’s views on vaccines are not always top of mind, even for self-described MAHA movement followers. An April 2026 survey of self-described MAHA voters found that just 10 percent identified re-evaluating vaccine safety as their top priority.

Nevertheless the number of parents opting their children out of vaccines continues to grow across the country. Data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention indicate that vaccine exemptions grew in 41 states and the District of Columbia between the 2024 and 2025 school years.

Even if Democrats can convince a sizable group of Republicans to trust their vaccine advice over Kennedy’s, a small and growing number of vaccine skeptics can cause public health havoc.

Though Andrews was able to convince more than 1 million South Carolinians to support her pro-science message, it was a relatively small group of vaccine skeptics in Spartanburg County, in the northwestern corner of the state, that prompted the state’s 2025 measles outbreak, which at the time was the largest in the United States since measles was formally eliminated in 2000. (Pennsylvania’s current outbreak has since topped South Carolina’s record, with more than 1,500 cases.)

There are some signs that pro-vaccine messages are beginning to resonate in these communities. Andrews’ message of impeaching RFK received an ovation in Spartanburg County during the campaign, and she did perform better there than Democratic candidates of the past. But as of now, the region still has a vaccination rate low enough that it is vulnerable to continued resurgences of measles.

As Andrews acknowledged in an op-ed during the campaign: “Trust doesn’t snap back like a rubber band. It takes years to build and minutes to burn.”

#5723. Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them

Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative way to turn a chemical produced by cancer cells into a weapon against them. Instead of delivering toxic drugs throughout the body, their experimental approach uses carbon monoxide released by cancer cells to manufacture anticancer compounds directly inside the cells themselves.

The research, led by Katsunori Tanaka at the RIKEN Pioneering Research Institute (PRI) in Japan, was published in Nature Communications. In laboratory experiments, the team demonstrated that a specially designed compound could trigger drug production inside cancer cells without generating the same toxic substances in healthy cells. Although the technique is still at an early stage, it could eventually provide a way to attack tumors while reducing the harmful side effects associated with conventional cancer treatments.

Turning Cancer's Own Toxic Gas Against It

One of the greatest challenges in cancer treatment is destroying malignant cells without damaging healthy tissue. Traditional chemotherapy can cause serious side effects because its toxic effects are not always limited to tumors. Tanaka and other researchers are investigating more selective strategies that could make cancer treatments safer.

Their long-term goal is to replace the direct delivery of toxic drugs with relatively harmless compounds that become active only after entering cancer cells. These compounds would use substances already present inside tumors to generate therapeutic drugs exactly where they are needed.

Carbon monoxide offers an intriguing opportunity for this approach. Although best known as a poisonous gas produced by sources such as gasoline engines, carbon monoxide is also generated naturally by many types of cancer cells. Because tumors can produce unusually high amounts of the gas, it may serve as a useful biological marker for identifying cancer cells, provided it can be detected.

Scientists in RIKEN's Biofunctional Synthetic Chemistry Laboratory investigated whether they could exploit this difference. Their strategy involved delivering a metal catalyst into cells and using the excess carbon monoxide in cancer cells to drive a chemical reaction that produces a toxic compound. In principle, the reaction would occur primarily in cancer cells, where enough carbon monoxide is available, while sparing normal cells.

Protecting the Catalyst Inside Cancer Cells

To make the system work, the researchers turned to a class of compounds known as palladacycles. These metal-containing compounds can react with carbon monoxide to produce an organic molecule called phenanthridinone. Certain derivatives of phenanthridinone are toxic to cells and have already been incorporated into anticancer drugs.

However, there was a major obstacle. When palladacycles are introduced directly into cells, substances such as glutathione rapidly deactivate their central palladium catalyst. Without an active catalyst, the reaction cannot produce the desired drug.

Tanaka's team addressed this problem by building on its previous work using metal catalysts to carry out chemical reactions in living systems. The researchers enclosed a palladacycle within albumin, a protein commonly found in blood. This protective protein carrier allows the complex to travel through the bloodstream while shielding the palladium catalyst from substances that would otherwise deactivate it after entering cells.

Laboratory Tests Reveal Selective Drug Production

The scientists evaluated their system through a series of experiments. They began by testing different palladacycles to identify which one could generate the greatest amount of phenanthridinone.

Next, they exposed cultured human liver, cervical, breast, and lung cancer cells to the albumin and palladacycle complex for 48 hours. They also tested the compound on a noncancerous cell line to determine whether the same chemical reaction would occur in healthy cells.

After 48 hours, the researchers detected phenanthridinone in the cancer cell lines but not in the normal cells. The findings indicated that the albumin carrier successfully protected the catalyst from glutathione and that the chemical reaction occurred selectively in the cancer cells under the conditions tested.

The team then refined the system so that the newly formed compound could separate from the carrier and move freely throughout the cell. Additional modifications allowed the reaction to generate a particularly toxic phenanthridinone derivative already used in anticancer drugs.

When the researchers introduced this modified system into cultured liver cancer cells, they observed the anticancer compound forming inside the cells. The cells subsequently showed signs of damage caused by the toxic drug, providing proof that the approach could generate a cancer-fighting substance directly within its intended target.

Why the Experimental Drug Did Not Form in Blood

An important safety concern involved carbon monoxide already present in the bloodstream. If that gas triggered the chemical reaction before the compound reached cancer cells, the resulting drug could damage blood cells instead of its intended target.

Fortunately, laboratory testing showed that the toxic drug was not produced in blood. The researchers believe this is because carbon monoxide in the bloodstream is largely attached to hemoglobin, the protein responsible for transporting oxygen. In this bound form, the gas appears to be unavailable for the reaction needed to manufacture the drug.

The finding suggests that the system may be able to travel through blood without prematurely generating harmful substances, although further studies will be needed to establish its safety in living organisms.

"This work represents an important advance in therapeutic in vivo synthetic chemistry," says Tanaka. "In our therapeutic strategy, molecules naturally present or generated within the body -- including disease-associated metabolites -- are used as endogenous chemical feedstocks to synthesize therapeutic molecules directly at the site of disease."

The researchers now plan to move beyond cultured cells and test the approach in animal models. If future experiments are successful, the technology could help establish a new class of cancer treatments that exploit the chemistry of tumors to produce drugs directly at the disease site, potentially limiting damage to healthy tissue.

#5722. Duet nabs $15M series A, plans to launch first NP-led ACO in 2027

Duet nabs $15M series A, plans to launch first NP-led ACO in 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Nurse practitioner-owned primary care practice network Duet secured $15 million in series A funding to expand its clinic network and grow its partnerships and team.

Kairos led the funding round, with participation from Lerer Hippeau.

Kairos co-founder and co-CEO Alex Fiance said in a statement the company is “one of those rare businesses where everybody wins.”

“It reaches patients in need, helps clinicians become business owners, and brings costs down for the payers and the U.S. government by catching problems early,” Fiance said. “We believe Duet has the potential to reshape care across the country in a highly scalable way and are excited to help fuel their growth.”

Duet is the largest network of independent NP-owned primary care practices in the U.S., the company says. It helps practices earn compensation through its various partnerships with insurers, including Anthem, Cigna and Centene.

Duet Founder and CEO Jonathan Goldberg told Fierce Healthcare the company’s platform “combines practice advisors with AI-powered tools” to offload administrative work and give NPs more time for patient care.

“Our technology identifies people who are drifting out of care and gets them scheduled. It threads together patient data ahead of every visit, so an NP knows who is at risk and what to focus on,” Goldberg said. “And we help extend care into the home for those who need extra attention with remote technology and wraparound support.”

Goldberg continued, “There’s a lot stacked against small practices. Our mission is to help NPs show up for people that the system has overlooked.”

Patients visiting Duet clinics had an overall NPS of 92 across approximately 400,000 visits a year, Goldberg said.

“Patients often comment that this is the first time they felt heard, had someone take the time to read through their chart, or had a condition diagnosed that other clinicians had dismissed,” Goldberg said. “The clinical results follow from that. Practices that join Duet see preventive screenings for conditions like breast cancer and colon cancer rise 30%, and ER visits fall 20%. We also bring back 25% of the patients who are unengaged, and those are the patients who tend to end up worse off.”

The company has raised $22.5 million to date and works with more than 130 clinics across 21 states, executives say.

Goldberg said the company plans to use the fresh capital in three main ways: serve more clinics, deepen its value-based care partnerships with insurers and add engineers to its team. He added that Duet is launching an accelerator program in 2027 to help clinics “start strong.

Alongside the funding round, Duet announced it plans to launch the first-ever NP-led Medicare Accountable Care Organization (ACO) in 2027.

NPs will design and govern the company’s new model, which Goldberg says will allow practice owners to maintain “their autonomy while getting the technology and resources to strengthen their care.”

“NPs already practice prevention first, and this gives them a way to be recognized for it,” he said.
