#5675. Amanda Seyfried Reveals What It Was Like To Be in Elizabeth Holmes’ Texas Home While the Theranos Founder Was in Prison

This article contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything.”

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary “You Can See Everything” gives viewers an unprecedented look into the home life of Elizabeth Holmes.

The disgraced Theranos founder invited the filmmakers to document the 34 days before she reported to the Federal Prison Camp in Bryan, TX, on May 30, 2023. Two years later, the A24 production team would pick up cameras again, joining Holmes’ partner, Billy Evans, and the couple’s two young children at their home in Austin, TX.

In a surprise twist to viewers, Amanda Seyfried, who portrayed Holmes in the Hulu miniseries “The Dropout,” becomes an important part of the narrative in the second half of the documentary.

The actress opened up about the experience in a Rolling Stone interview with Fielder and Oppenheim, and described what it was really like to enter the family’s Texas home while Holmes was away in prison.

Seyfried—who had been shown footage Fielder and Oppenheim captured in the days leading up to Holmes reporting to prison—explained that she had some preconceived notions about Evans.

She chose to put those feelings aside before visiting the home—a four-bedroom, three-bathroom luxury residence that’s currently on the market for $2.25 million with Amy Deane of Moreland Properties.

“I wanted to turn my disdain off a little bit, because I’m in his house now with his children—with their children,” she emphasized. “I always want to give people the benefit of the doubt, and I felt bad that I had talked a bunch of sh-t about him up until that point.”

The “Mamma Mia!” star noted that although she didn’t particularly “like” Evans, she was careful with her words because she was “coming into this man’s house.”

She explained that “trying to engage with Billy” was “going fine” until he received an unexpected call from Holmes.

“That was just ... what an experience for somebody to have, to say the least,” she reflected, adding that everything she felt was plainly visible on her face in that scene.

“We didn’t know she was gonna call right then. I am sitting there with her children and cuddling with her dog! While she’s in prison!” the star recalled.

Later, the documentary would show Fielder, Seyfried, and Evans having dinner together—a moment that grew tense quickly, due to a stark difference in political opinions between Seyfried and Evans.

“I don’t want to provoke him, but at this point, it’s kind of like, the gloves are off,” she recalled. “I was in the frame of mind where I’m like, ‘OK, this guy is disrespectful, and I’m here in his home, I’m gonna argue this because I actually have a pretty solid stance on things.’”

Seyfried revealed that the dynamic was difficult to balance, as she was torn between being “protective” of herself and “trying to set the record straight,” but she was also hoping to maintain “some kind of rapport” with Evans, so filming could resume in the home without the entire production crew getting kicked out.

The documentary eventually leverages Seyfried’s acting skills—and unique knowledge of the source material—to create a series of reenactments to key the audience into moments that happened before cameras picked up.

These reenactments would take Seyfried and the crew to the ultraprivate Del Mar, CA, beach home Holmes had rented in the weeks leading up to her prison stay.

In the Rolling Stone interview, Fielder remarked that Seyfried had been very “curious” about the objects that were found on the re-creation sets, and wanted to learn which items were placed by the production design team and which had existed in the home when Holmes lived there two years earlier.

“I was just grasping at anything that could ground me back into this world, because it had been so long, and I think I was also experiencing some kind of weird, like, meta-vortex, because I had just seen Elizabeth Holmes in this house, and the house is so specific,” Seyfried explained.

The four-bedroom, four-bathroom home certainly is specific, and became an instantly recognizable location from the moment the “You Can See Everything” trailer dropped. It’s one of just about a dozen residences in the ultraexclusive community called Sandy Lane, about a half-hour from San Diego.

The single-story home was built in 1948 and includes direct access to a private beach. It features tall ceilings, exposed beams, and sizable windows that connect the moody space to its serene surroundings.

The actress said it was “just crazy” to be in the “same place” she had seen Holmes in, through footage Fielder and his team had previously captured.

“Nobody had been in Holmes and Evans’ beach house for two years, or whatever,” she said. “And suddenly, it’s like I’ve time-traveled two years into the past.”

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

AMA President Willie Underwood III, M.D., said in a statement that "patients deserve to know who is responsible for their care."

"Physicians also need the authority, oversight and liability protections to make independent decisions when AI is part of the care team," Underwood said.

Kouper's AI agents work inside health system electronic health record (EHR) systems like Athenahealth and Epic to coordinate care from scheduling through discharge and follow-up.

The deal pairs Ellipsis's "emotionally intelligent" AI voice care manager, Sage, with Kouper's native EHR integrations and longitudinal patient maps to deliver continuous, connected patient care, according to the companies.

Founded in 2022, Kouper has raised funding from investors including CVS Health Ventures, General Catalyst and 25madison. Ellipsis' Sage can pick up from there with discharge follow-ups, medication adherence support and clinical check-ins by phone and text. “Healthcare has enormous potential to benefit from AI, but the hard part has been making that technology work for patients and care teams,” said Mainul Mondal, founder and CEO of Ellipsis Health, in a statement. “We have extraordinary clinicians, but we can’t solve access and continuity problems by asking them to do more. Kouper brings critical infrastructure for making that possible inside health systems. By combining their native integrations and longitudinal patient maps with Sage’s emotional intelligence, we can help care teams extend their reach and deliver more continuous, personalized support.”

#5673. Low testosterone linked to 18% higher risk of dying from cancer

Men with very low testosterone levels may face an increased risk of developing cancer and dying from the disease later in life, according to a major international study. The findings suggest that testosterone levels could provide an early clue to future health risks, potentially years or even decades before cancer is diagnosed.

Researchers found that men with low testosterone had an 18 percent higher risk of dying from cancer. However, the relationship was not the same for every type of cancer. Surprisingly, testosterone levels were not associated with prostate cancer risk. Instead, prostate cancer was more closely linked to low levels of two other hormones, sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and luteinizing hormone.

The research comes from the Androgens In Men Study (AIMS), an international collaboration led by Professor Bu Yeap at The University of Western Australia. The project investigates how different sex hormones relate to cancer risk and other health outcomes in men.

Study Tracks Testosterone and Cancer Risk in 26,000 Men

Published in the journal Lancet Healthy Longevity, the study examined data from more than 26,000 men participating in 11 long-running studies across Australia, the United States, and Europe.

Researchers analyzed hormone concentrations in blood samples collected earlier in the men's lives. They then compared those measurements with cancer diagnoses and deaths recorded over the following decades, allowing them to investigate whether hormone levels were associated with future cancer outcomes.

The analysis included testosterone, dihydrotestosterone (DHT), SHBG, and luteinizing hormone. Luteinizing hormone is produced by the pituitary gland and signals the testes to produce testosterone.

"We wanted to know whether the concentration of these hormones in the blood was related to the risk of men being diagnosed with, or dying from, cancer into the future," Professor Yeap said.

"What we saw was that if a man had low testosterone levels - in the lowest one-fifth compared to the highest one-fifth of the range - their subsequent risk of dying from cancer was higher, even after allowing for age and other health-related factors."

Cancer Risk Increased Below a Key Testosterone Level

The researchers identified a testosterone concentration below which cancer risk began to rise. According to Professor Yeap, testosterone levels in healthy younger men typically range from 10 to 30 nanomoles per liter (nmol/L), although concentrations generally decrease with age.

Testosterone levels can also be influenced by factors that people may be able to change, including body mass index and physical activity. Certain medical conditions, such as diabetes, can affect testosterone concentrations as well.

"We saw that when baseline testosterone was below 8.6 nmol/L, subsequent cancer risk started increasing," Professor Yeap said.

"This suggests low testosterone is an important biomarker, so it's possible that looking at testosterone levels could help us identify men who might do poorly if they get cancer down the track."

These findings raise the possibility that testosterone measurements could help doctors recognize men who may face greater health risks in the future. However, the results show an association and do not establish that low testosterone itself causes cancer.

A Surprising Finding About Prostate Cancer

Because testosterone plays an important role in male reproductive health, researchers also investigated whether naturally occurring testosterone levels influenced the likelihood of developing prostate cancer.

The question has particular medical significance because lowering testosterone is an established treatment for prostate cancer. However, the new analysis found no evidence that a man's natural testosterone concentration was associated with his risk of developing the disease.

"Since reducing testosterone levels is a treatment for prostate cancer there's always been a question of whether the amount of testosterone your own body makes relates to your risk of prostate cancer but based on our findings there's no evidence they are related," Professor Yeap said.

"We did find, however, that men with low levels of SHBG and luteinizing hormone were at higher risk of prostate cancer."

The results highlight an important distinction between testosterone and other hormones involved in male reproductive function. Although low testosterone was associated with higher overall cancer risk and mortality, prostate cancer showed a different pattern of hormonal associations.

Why Low Testosterone Does Not Mean Men Need Supplements

Despite the connection between low testosterone and cancer outcomes, Professor Yeap emphasized that the findings should not be interpreted as a recommendation to take testosterone supplements to prevent cancer.

"While we've shown low levels are associated with increased risk, we haven't got any evidence yet that actually giving men testosterone will reduce that risk," he said.

Instead, unexpectedly low testosterone could be a reason to investigate a person's overall health. A medical evaluation may uncover underlying conditions or risk factors that require attention, even when there is no evidence of a problem affecting the testes.

"What we would say to men is if they are found for whatever reason to be low in testosterone, it's important to go to the doctor for a full checkup. It may not show any sign of testicular disease, but it might show other health issues or risk factors they need to address.

"It could be a wake-up call and encouragement for men to engage in more healthy lifestyle behaviors, and to get regular, holistic checkups to stay on top of their health."

#5672. 5 takeaways from STAT’s investigation of the sprawling ‘three-parent IVF’ industry

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Megan covers the intersection of science and society. How is biomedical research funded? Who benefits? And how do new technologies reflect and shape our values? You can reach Megan on Signal at mmolteni.13.

The investigation started with a tip from a British couple.

After trying to have a second child for several years, they had signed up with a U.S.-based company called International Fertility Group (IFG), paying tens of thousands of dollars for access abroad to an experimental fertility procedure illegal in the U.S. and tightly regulated in the U.K. The procedure, known as MRT — for mitochondrial replacement techniques — is sometimes called “three-parent IVF,” because it involves creating embryos that combine the genes of a mother and father with a bit of DNA from the mitochondria of a third person.

In the U.K., MRT is allowed at only one academic medical center, and only for the purposes of lowering the risk of passing on mitochondrial disease. But according to IFG, the procedure could also help older women overcome issues that make the odds of IVF go down significantly after the age of 40. Despite being a doctor herself, the woman in the couple had been taken in by the hope of a miracle.

Her husband reached out to me concerned the claims were unfounded, and hoping STAT could look into it.

Over the past eight months, my reporting took me inside an emerging international MRT tourism industry. It led me to IFG’s headquarters in an office park outside of Chicago and to one of its partners in Albania, an upscale fertility clinic where a Turkish embryologist living in Slovakia would fly in monthly to perform the procedure on IFG clients’ eggs or embryos. With the help of an Albanian journalist, Inva Hasanaliaj, we dug into corporate registration and medical licensing records. Freelance science reporter Edward Chen helped us to gather the stories of current and former IFG clients and interview scientists, including the world’s top MRT researchers.

All of this reporting was undertaken in an effort to understand what is driving demand for this unproven procedure, what risks women are taking to seek it out, and how commercial claims stack up against the science. Here’s what we found.

Currently, there are no peer-reviewed studies in humans supporting the idea that MRT can overcome infertility issues caused by aging, especially in women 35 years and older. A pilot study from a fertility clinic in Greece, published in 2023, reported that MRT could improve live birth rates for women under the age of 40, but the biggest improvements occurred among the youngest patients. For the 12 patients who were 39 at the time of MRT, the live birth rate was less than 10%.

Researchers affiliated with IFG did present some data in a conference abstract for a 2025 European scientific meeting, claiming that among 66 patients with a mean age of 39, live birth rates following MRT reached rates of 40% or higher. But scientists told STAT the abstract lacked key information required to support that claim, and a conference organizer questioned whether it should have been accepted.

The most compelling evidence it might work in older women comes from a single lab study in mice. But even the underlying hypothesis that mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to age-related infertility is supported by very little direct evidence, experts told STAT.

Before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Kyiv was poised to become the MRT capital of the world. Women traveled from Europe, Israel, and the U.S. to at least three clinics there offering it as an infertility treatment. Unpublished data from the Nadiya Clinic — the most advanced operation in Kyiv — shows that a form of MRT called pronuclear transfer did not improve the odds of IVF for older women. Among 19 patients aged 36 to 44, only one gave birth to a baby following pronuclear transfer.

In contrast, among 10 infertile patients under the age of 35, MRT resulted in nine live births.

For the past few years, International Fertility Group has advertised its MRT program as “a groundbreaking fertility treatment that offers renewed hope to women with advanced maternal age or a history of failed cycles.” The company’s social media posts about MRT frequently targeted women over the age of 35, and its own internal data showed its clients were skewing older. According to an IFG webinar from February, the average age of a patient in the company’s MRT program was 39.2 years old in 2022; last year it was 45.6 years old.

After STAT contacted IFG about these materials, which several experts described as “misleading” and “unethical,” the company removed them. In a statement, IFG acknowledged that the evidence for MRT remains limited and emphasized that its role is to provide nonmedical support to patients. “IFG does not characterize innovative treatment as guaranteed, routine, or risk-free,” the statement said. “Patients are not promised a pregnancy, a live birth, or any particular outcome.”

The company’s MRT program is currently on pause. Last week, hours after STAT’s investigation was published, Birol Aydin, the Turkish embryologist who performed the procedure for IFG clients in Albania, announced on LinkedIn that he was stepping back from clinical work to focus on research.

Clinics unaffiliated with IFG operating in Mexico and the Bahamas are continuing to market MRT as a fertility treatment to women 40 and older as a way to combat age-related declines in egg quality. Neither has published any outcome data.

The concerns are twofold. First, that companies are profiting from selling false hope to people with a strong desire to try everything possible to have genetically related children. And second, that children born through commercial MRT won’t be monitored for any adverse health effects that might emerge later in their lives.

Data from the Nadiya Clinic underscore similar results from that 2023 pilot study in Greece, showing that a different form of MRT, called maternal spindle transfer, could help women under the age of 35 with a history of severe infertility get pregnant and have children.

Researchers at Ghent University are currently launching a small study of MRT for addressing these types of fertility failures, which collectively are called OZEMA (for oocyte, zygote, and embryo maturation arrest). Initial results are expected sometime next year. Positive outcomes would add to the increasing pressure to ease restrictions on human trials of MRT for infertility in countries where such studies are currently banned, including the U.S., so that people don’t have to go abroad.

#5670. Magic mushrooms rewire the brain in a way scientists didn't expect

A new study from the University of California, Santa Cruz, has revealed how psilocybin, the psychedelic substance found in "magic mushrooms," changes the brain by reorganizing connections between nerve cells. The findings could eventually help scientists develop treatments for mental health conditions that capture some of psilocybin's potential benefits without producing hallucinations.

The research, published October 15 in Nature Neuroscience, found that psilocybin rapidly encourages brain cells to form new connections and helps those connections mature. At the same time, it promotes the removal of certain older connections, suggesting that its effects involve more than simply increasing communication between neurons.

Experiments in mice also revealed something especially intriguing. The researchers were able to separate the cellular changes responsible for this rewiring from a behavioral response commonly associated with psychedelic effects. This suggests that some of psilocybin's effects on brain structure may be achievable without the hallucinations typically associated with the drug.

The discovery could provide a foundation for developing medications that enhance the brain's ability to adapt and reorganize itself, a property known as neuroplasticity. Such treatments might eventually offer new approaches for depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and other psychiatric conditions.

The team also identified a particular group of neurons in the cerebral cortex that plays an essential role in psilocybin's effects on brain connections. Importantly, the researchers discovered that the drug does not affect every brain in the same way. Its influence depends partly on whether the brain has previously experienced chronic stress.

"I consider this work a major advance, particularly in our understanding of how psilocybin reshapes neural circuits and its potential implications for treating mental disorders," said senior author Yi Zuo, professor of molecular, cell, and developmental biology at UC Santa Cruz.

Why Scientists Are Taking a New Look at Psychedelics

Scientific interest in psychedelic drugs has changed dramatically over the past century. During the middle of the 20th century, substances such as psilocybin and LSD attracted attention from Western researchers because of their powerful effects on perception, consciousness, and mood.

Early studies suggested these compounds might have applications in psychiatric treatment. However, scientific investigations slowed substantially after the United States passed the Controlled Substances Act in 1970, which imposed strict restrictions on these substances.

In recent years, researchers have renewed their interest in psychedelics, particularly their ability to produce rapid and potentially lasting changes in brain function.

Scientists sometimes describe these compounds as "psychoplastogens" because they can stimulate neuroplasticity after a single dose. Neuroplasticity refers to the brain's capacity to change its structure and activity by forming, strengthening, reorganizing, or removing connections between neurons.

This property is particularly interesting for mental health treatment because conditions such as depression can involve disruptions in the circuits responsible for regulating mood, emotions, and behavior.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has previously recognized the therapeutic potential of psychedelic research by granting Breakthrough Therapy designations to substances including psilocybin and MDMA. These designations are intended to accelerate the development and review of promising treatments for serious medical conditions.

In September 2026, the FDA took another step toward evaluating psychedelic treatments by organizing a public hearing titled "Considerations for Potential Future Therapeutic Use of Psychedelic Drugs."

Experts discussed how healthcare professionals administering psychedelic treatments should be qualified, how potential risks could be managed through Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) programs, and how future clinical trials should be designed.

As regulators examine ways psychedelic treatments might eventually become part of mainstream healthcare, researchers are increasingly focused on understanding exactly what these substances do to the brain. Identifying the cellular mechanisms behind their effects could help scientists develop treatments that are both effective and safer to administer.

To investigate how psilocybin changes brain structure, the UC Santa Cruz team used an advanced imaging method called two-photon microscopy.

This technology allows scientists to observe extremely small structures inside living tissue with remarkable detail. Using it, the researchers followed individual connections on neurons in living mice over several weeks, allowing them to see how those structures changed after psilocybin treatment.

Their attention centered on tiny projections called dendritic spines. These structures extend from neurons and receive messages from neighboring nerve cells. They help form synapses, the specialized junctions through which neurons communicate.

Synapses are essential for processing information and supporting functions such as learning, memory, and emotional regulation. Changes in their number, strength, and organization can alter the way information travels through the brain.

Within just 24 hours of psilocybin administration, the researchers observed a substantial increase in newly forming dendritic spines.

But the drug did more than encourage new connections to appear. It also helped them develop into more mature structures at an unusually rapid pace.

Normally, newly formed spines often begin as small, immature structures described as "stubby." Many remain unstable and disappear before becoming fully developed connections.

After psilocybin treatment, however, a much larger proportion developed into structures with a distinctive "mushroom" appearance. These mature spines are generally more stable and contain higher concentrations of receptors that receive chemical signals from neighboring neurons.

Because of these features, mature spines can support stronger and more persistent communication between brain cells, potentially contributing to lasting changes in circuits involved in memory and mood.

For lead author Jacob Baker, one of the biggest questions is whether these structural changes require the intense psychedelic experience typically produced by psilocybin.

"Psychedelics are fascinating compounds because they have the potential to profoundly transform who we are by reshaping the neural circuits in our brains," said Baker, a Ph.D. student in Zuo's lab.

"These newly formed connections can integrate into existing neural circuitry and persist over time, leaving a lasting structural trace of psilocybin's effects on the brain."

Psilocybin Affects Healthy and Stressed Brains Differently

One of the study's most revealing findings was that psilocybin's influence on brain connections changed depending on whether the mice had experienced prolonged stress.

In healthy mice, psilocybin initially stimulated the formation of new dendritic spines. Over the following three weeks, however, the number of connections gradually moved back toward its previous level.

This happened partly because the brain eliminated some connections that had existed before treatment. Rather than simply accumulating additional synapses, the healthy brain appeared to reorganize its existing circuitry while maintaining an overall balance.

The researchers observed a different response in mice exposed to chronic stress.

To investigate this, they used an unpredictable mild stress model, which exposes animals to varying low-intensity stressors and produces changes that resemble certain features of human depression.

Prolonged stress is known to interfere with neural communication and can cause substantial losses of synaptic connections. Over time, these changes can weaken the circuits involved in important brain functions.

When the stressed mice received psilocybin, the researchers observed an especially strong increase in the formation of new dendritic spines.

At the same time, psilocybin prevented the unusually high rate of connection loss associated with chronic stress.

Together, these effects suggest that psilocybin may do more than temporarily increase the number of connections in the brain. Under stressful conditions, it may also help preserve existing connections and restore circuitry that has been disrupted.

"These findings challenge the prevailing view that psilocybin simply increases neural connectivity and suggest that its effects depend on the brain's underlying condition," Zuo added.

"This provides a new perspective on how psychedelics might help restore neural circuits disrupted by stress, with potentially important implications for understanding their therapeutic effects in depression and other psychiatric disorders."

Could Psilocybin Rewire the Brain Without Hallucinations?

Perhaps the most significant implication of the research concerns a longstanding question in psychedelic medicine: Are hallucinations and altered states of consciousness necessary for the brain changes that might contribute to therapeutic benefits?

To explore this possibility, the scientists examined the role of serotonin 2A receptors (5-HT2ARs), which are proteins on the surfaces of cells that respond to chemical signals. These receptors are central to the effects of psilocybin and other classic psychedelics.

The researchers focused on a group of nerve cells called Layer 5 pyramidal neurons. These cells are located in the cerebral cortex, the outer region of the brain involved in complex functions such as perception, reasoning, and decision-making.

Layer 5 pyramidal neurons serve as important communication pathways that send information from the cortex to other brain regions. They also contain high levels of serotonin 2A receptors, making them especially relevant to understanding psilocybin's effects.

Using genetically modified mice, the team selectively changed whether these neurons possessed the receptors.

The results revealed a striking separation between changes in brain connections and a behavior associated with psychedelic activity.

When the researchers restored serotonin 2A receptors only in Layer 5 pyramidal neurons, psilocybin was still able to stimulate the development of new synapses and help stabilize them.

Surprisingly, these mice did not display the characteristic head twitch response that researchers commonly use as an indicator of psychedelic activity in rodents.

The scientists then performed the opposite experiment.

When they removed serotonin 2A receptors specifically from Layer 5 pyramidal neurons, psilocybin lost its ability to stimulate the same structural growth of synapses.

However, the mice still exhibited the head twitch response.

These contrasting results demonstrate that serotonin 2A receptor signaling in Layer 5 pyramidal neurons is necessary and sufficient for the structural brain changes observed in the experiments, while those same receptors are not required for the psychedelic-associated behavioral response.

In other words, the cellular pathway responsible for psilocybin's brain rewiring can be separated from the pathway responsible for this particular behavioral marker of psychedelic activity.

Because mice cannot describe subjective experiences, the head twitch response does not directly establish whether an animal is experiencing hallucinations. Nevertheless, the findings provide important evidence that these two effects involve distinct cellular mechanisms.

A Potential Path Toward Psychedelic Treatments Without the Trip

The discovery could have major implications for the development of future psychiatric medications.

If researchers can identify compounds that activate the brain's ability to rebuild and reorganize neural connections without triggering psychedelic effects, it may become possible to create treatments that preserve some of psilocybin's therapeutic potential while avoiding the need for patients to undergo intense altered states of consciousness.

Such medications could be easier to administer and might require less intensive clinical supervision than conventional psychedelic-assisted therapies.

"By showing that therapeutic circuit remodeling and hallucinogenic effects operate through distinct cellular pathways, our study provides a promising blueprint for designing non-hallucinogenic drug analogs," Zuo said.

"Such therapeutics could deliver the fast and lasting antidepressant benefits of psychedelics while eliminating hallucinogenic side effects -- making neuroplasticity treatments safer, more scalable, and accessible to a broader patient population."

Although the results are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice. Additional research will be necessary to determine whether the same cellular mechanisms operate in humans and whether separating brain rewiring from psychedelic effects can produce effective treatments for depression, PTSD, or other psychiatric disorders.

For now, the findings provide a more detailed picture of how psilocybin changes the brain and reveal a potential strategy for harnessing its effects on neural connections without relying on the psychedelic experience itself.

The study's other UC Santa Cruz coauthors include molecular and cell biologists Jacob Baker, Emily Kogan, Shaorong Ma, and Ju Lu, alongside Zuo.

Funding came from the National Institute of Mental Health and the National Institute on Aging. The psilocybin used in the experiments was supplied through the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) Drug Supply Program.

#5669. What’s Next for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac After the Midterm Elections

President Donald Trump has suggested that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac's government conservatorship should end. But whether that will happen under his administration remains unclear after the midterms.

Since the federal bailout in 2008, Fannie and Freddie have remained under conservatorship for 18 years, with the terms subjecting them to strict oversight and regulation by the Federal Housing Finance Agency.

For years, the U.S. Treasury has collected nearly all profits from the two entities, an amount surpassing $300 billion and exceeding the government's outlay in the bailout. Trump has floated the idea of ending the conservatorship since his first term in office, an idea that regained attention when he returned to the White House in 2025.

Trump suggested this could mean an initial public offering of the two mortgage giants, with both companies valued at up to $1 trillion combined and selling between 5% and 15% of their stock.

Key Democrats have expressed reservations about privatizing Fannie and Freddie or otherwise ending the conservatorship, raising questions about whether the Trump administration will pursue the matter with Democrats in control of Congress.

Trump has said little about the matter in recent months. Billionaire investor Bill Ackman, who has long pushed for an end to conservatorship, believes that the Trump administration wanted to wait until after the midterms to take action.

“The reason why it’s not being touched right now is, you know, midterms,” he told CNBC on Election Day.

Before the election, a senior Trump administration official said the end of conservatorship for Fannie and Freddie could still be on. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggested the government could take up the matter again in 2027 or 2028.

U.S. Federal Housing Finance Agency Director William Pulte supported the idea this spring. He said that changes to their credit scoring requirements introduced this year could increase the chances of success. But only Trump knew the timing, he said.

“We stand ready every day to execute the president’s vision, and if and when he decides he wants to do something, we are locked and loaded and ready to go," Pulte said.

But starting in January, the Trump administration may face stiff opposition in Congress to privatizing Fannie and Freddie, a move that many economists have warned could put upward pressure on mortgage rates.

Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA), who's running to chair the House Financial Services Committee, has consistently opposed administrative efforts by regulators to rapidly release Fannie and Freddie from conservatorship without comprehensive congressional oversight, public transparency, and safeguards for affordable housing and racial equity.

"To address the affordable housing crisis, Congress must ensure that Fannie and Freddie meet their mission to provide liquidity, sustainability, and affordability to all housing markets in the U.S., and at all times," Waters said at a hearing in April.

Legal and political analysts are divided on whether the executive branch could end the conservatorship by fiat, but such a push would almost certainly face stiff opposition from Democrats in Congress.

The White House didn't respond to a Realtor.com® request for comment about the future of the conservatorship. Waters also didn't respond.

Even as he discussed the end of conservatorship, Trump used Fannie and Freddie as tools to try to help improve affordability in the market. That meant directing them to purchase $200 billion in mortgage-backed securities in an effort to improve the housing market.

Trump's former Federal Housing Commissioner Frank Cassidy told Realtor.com that privatization is a lever Trump could pull without his party controlling Congress. But it needs to be structured in a way that benefits the market. One worry is that the lack of government backing would drive up mortgage rates.

"It hasn't been a priority yet. It would need to be worked on very quickly because it will take some time," Cassidy said. "How do you structure it in a way that makes it more favorable? The idea under conservatorship is implicitly a government guarantee."

In the meantime, the Mortgage Brokers of America reiterated that a positive outcome is still possible.

"MBA continues to believe that GSE release must preserve what works to ensure that it continues to deliver what consumers need and investors expect," it said. "And importantly, any release must include an explicit federal backstop—passed by Congress and paid for by the GSEs—of their mortgage-backed securities to protect consumers, taxpayers, and our best-in-the-world housing finance system."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5668. Dyania Health, Nvidia team up to bring clinical reasoning AI inside hospital networks

Dyania Health, Nvidia team up to bring clinical reasoning AI inside hospital networks" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Dyania Health is partnering with Nvidia to run its Synapsis AI clinical reasoning platform inside hospitals’ IT systems, enabling large-scale analysis without patient data leaving their networks.

The startup's Synapsis AI reads a patient's full medical record, including clinical notes, imaging and operative reports, labs and other largely unstructured information, and answers clinical questions while pointing back to supporting evidence in the chart. Dyania Health goes beyond summarizing medical records; it uses AI to convert messy, unstructured clinical records into usable datasets and insights.

Nvidia provides the computing infrastructure needed to perform that analysis across potentially entire patient populations behind the hospital firewall, without transferring patient records outside the health system, according to the company.

Dyania brings the clinical reasoning technology and implementation expertise, while Nvidia brings the accelerated computing platform and the software that lets it run securely and efficiently on-premises, Eirini Schlosser, founder and CEO of Dyania Health, told Fierce Healthcare.

Through this collaboration with Nvidia, Dyania's Synapsis AI could help health systems turn large volumes of unstructured clinical data into actionable insights at a scale that would be impractical with manual chart review, while keeping patient data inside the hospital’s own infrastructure, Schlosser said.

Health systems have vast amounts of valuable clinical information locked in unstructured medical records, but manually reviewing those records makes it difficult to use that data at scale for research, registries and predictive models. Synapsis AI aims to remove that bottleneck by analyzing patients’ records longitudinally, determining what happened and when, and identifying the clinical evidence supporting those conclusions, according to the company, which launched out of stealth two years ago.

Frontier models are becoming extraordinarily capable, but the architectures, training data sets, as well as logic are not built to perform clinical reasoning in a real-world healthcare system environment, Schlosser noted.

Dyania's Synapsis AI combines specialized models, a clinician-annotated clinical knowledge base, evidence tracing and hospital-specific implementation. Dyania says it has invested more than 25,000 physician hours annotating medical cases so that Synapsis AI can perform clinical reasoning. This specialized approach is better suited to complex clinical reasoning than a single general-purpose AI model, Schlosser asserted.

"Every patient's story is spread across years of notes, reports and results, and for the first time we can reason across all of it at once, the way a specialist does, for every patient in a health system rather than one chart at a time,” Schlosser said.

Synapsis AI is built on the Nvidia AI enterprise software stack end to end. Dyania trains its proprietary clinical models with the Nvidia NeMo framework for model training and reinforcement learning. Inside the health system, Synapsis AI runs on Nvidia TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM on the hospital's own accelerated computing infrastructure, so inference stays inside the hospital's private network.

Hospitals can use their own historical patient data to determine which treatments work for which patients, identify care gaps and ultimately recommend the next appropriate action, according to Schlosser.

Under the collaboration, the companies will work to bring Synapsis AI on Nvidia infrastructure to health systems in the U.S. and internationally, publish joint case studies and integrate Synapsis AI with Nvidia's healthcare software stack. The companies are exploring additional Nvidia technologies to secure AI processing, handle multiple clinical workloads at once and scale computing capacity, with the goal of moving from batch processing toward near-real-time clinical insights at the point of care.

"Health systems need AI they can trust, integrate into their workflows and operate efficiently. That means connecting information across clinical systems, validating performance for the patients they serve, protecting sensitive data and making results useful within the tools clinicians already use," Chelsea Sumner, Nvidia's U.S. healthcare AI startups ecosystem lead, told Fierce Healthcare.

"Dyania’s approach addresses part of that challenge by running inside the hospital’s own environment and linking findings to evidence in the patient record. Scaling also requires clinicians, technology teams and hospital leaders to work together from the start, with clear responsibility for reviewing results and monitoring performance. Success should be measured by whether AI helps teams find patients who need attention, make better-informed decisions and spend more time delivering care," Sumner said.

Cleveland Clinic used Dyania Health’s Synapsis AI, running on Nvidia infrastructure, to analyze up to 16 years of records from 7,812 aortic valve replacement patients. The study addressed a central concern for patients: How long will the replacement valve last and will another procedure be needed?

Researchers reviewed nearly 8,000 patient records between 2005 and 2021, mostly narrative notes and echocardiogram reports that registries can struggle to capture.

"Understanding how a replacement heart valve performs means following a patient across years of care, connecting the original operative report with subsequent progress notes, hospitalizations, echocardiograms, other medical conditions and later interventions. Much of that information is buried in narrative records that researchers would otherwise need to review manually," Schlosser noted.

The AI extracted information from narrative clinical records and answered 88 questions per patient about their valves, health conditions, and subsequent care. Each answer linked to supporting evidence in the chart, he noted.

Researchers used that dataset to build a predictive model of valve deterioration and the risk of another intervention. The model estimates valve deterioration and repeat-procedure risk at three, five and 10 years post-procedure, with estimates that update as new medical information about the patient becomes available.

"Historically, this would have required human manual abstraction, and for 7,812 patients it would be humanly impossible to read and abstract features on an ongoing basis at the rate at which medical records are changing. Additionally, humans reading a medical record can often miss information if they skim through it," Schlosser said.

The tool is used to help inform care but requires external validation from clinicians.

"Using technology to bring together and analyze information that can help us predict the duration of implanted heart valves is a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients," said Lars G. Svensson, M.D., Ph.D., chief of the Heart, Vascular and Thoracic Institute at Cleveland Clinic, in a statement.

The health system began working with Dyania Health a year ago to use its AI platform for clinical trial recruitment.

Synapsis AI made it possible for the first time to comprehensively analyze nearly two decades of patient data, Schlosser asserted. "What was even more groundbreaking was the ability to go from raw data in unstructured form to predictive risk models in one fell swoop. This enables precision care at scale and empowers physicians with stronger sets of information backing their clinical decisions about any given patient, including questions like 'when should the patient have their next echo?' or 'when will the patient likely need a reintervention?'" Schlosser said.

The Cleveland Clinic and Dyania Health collaboration reflects Nvidia's broader focus to provide healthcare and life sciences innovators the computing platform and AI tools to advance research and help care teams better understand patients’ needs, Sumner said.

The heart valve study shows how Synapsis AI could help health systems use their own patient data to determine which treatments work best for which patients and improve predictive models over time, ultimately supporting more personalized care recommendations, according to Dyania Health.

"Nvidia's infrastructure enables us to handle more work concurrently and use resources more efficiently. That could allow hospitals to examine larger populations, ask more detailed questions and revisit analyses more frequently. The longer-term opportunity is to move from periodic batches of records toward insights available closer to the moment a clinician needs them," Schlosser said.

"We can do that within the health system’s own environment, keeping patient records behind its firewall. We are also evaluating capabilities for distributed inference, workload isolation and protection of data during computation. Computing power alone does not make a clinical conclusion correct; it allows a carefully developed clinical system to work at greater scale and speed," he said.

Sumner asserts that healthcare organizations are just scratching the surface on the potential for AI to uncover clinically useful information buried in longitudinal patient records.

"Connecting a physician’s notes with earlier test results and treatment history could help identify patients who need follow-up, match people with clinical trials and give researchers a clearer understanding of how treatments perform over time," she said. "The Cleveland Clinic heart valve study is a concrete example. AI helped researchers assemble a detailed view of patients’ care to study how replacement valves deteriorate. The opportunity is to turn that knowledge into more personalized monitoring and better-informed care decisions. Clinicians need to be able to review the supporting evidence, validate the findings and decide what they mean for each patient."

#5667. MIT scientists turn immune cells into cancer killers inside the body

MIT researchers have developed a new technique that allows them to transform immune cells into cancer fighters directly inside the body, potentially making advanced treatments for cancer and autoimmune diseases much easier to produce and administer.

The method focuses on natural killer (NK) cells, a type of immune cell that can be engineered to recognize and destroy harmful cells. These include cancerous T cells and T cells that mistakenly attack healthy tissue, contributing to conditions such as lymphoma and autoimmune hepatitis.

Rather than extracting immune cells from a patient and modifying them in a laboratory, the researchers use tiny particles made of fatty molecules to deliver genetic instructions directly to NK cells. These instructions, carried by messenger RNA, tell the cells to produce specialized proteins that help them identify and eliminate diseased T cells.

The resulting cells, known as CAR NK cells, could eventually be used against several different diseases. By carrying out the engineering process inside the body, the new approach could eliminate much of the time, expense, and complexity involved in manufacturing personalized immune cell therapies.

"The manufacturing challenges with CAR NK cells are significant. The idea here is you can deliver a nanoparticle that will modify your own NK cells with a CAR construct and teach them to attack tumor cells," says Daniel Anderson, a professor in MIT's Department of Chemical Engineering and a member of MIT's Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research and Institute for Medical Engineering and Science.

Anderson is the senior author of the research, published in Nature Biotechnology. The lead authors are MIT postdoctoral researcher Yuang Chen and graduate students Julia Monkovic and Haseeb Mughal. Robert Langer, MIT's David H. Koch Institute Professor, also contributed to the study.

Why Current Cancer Immunotherapies Are So Complex

Immune cell engineering has already transformed treatment options for certain cancers. During the past decade, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved seven cancer therapies that use genetically modified T cells, known as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells.

These treatments work by equipping T cells with specially designed receptors that recognize particular markers, or antigens, on other cells. When an engineered T cell encounters its designated target, such as a protein associated with cancer, it becomes activated and attacks the cell carrying that marker.

CAR T cell therapies have been especially effective against blood cancers arising from B cells. These include certain forms of leukemia and lymphoma, as well as multiple myeloma.

However, preparing these treatments involves several complicated steps. Doctors first collect blood from the patient and send it to a specialized facility. There, technicians separate the T cells, genetically modify them to produce the desired receptors, and grow enough engineered cells for treatment. The finished cells must then be transported back to the hospital and infused into the patient.

Natural Killer Cells Offer a Different Way to Fight Cancer

Scientists have recently been exploring whether natural killer cells could be engineered in a similar way. One important advantage is their potential to treat cancers and autoimmune conditions involving abnormal T cells.

Trying to use CAR T cells against diseased T cells creates a major problem. Because both the engineered cells and their intended targets are T cells, the modified cells may recognize and destroy one another. This unintended attack can undermine the treatment.

Natural killer cells avoid this complication because they are a different type of immune cell. They can be programmed to attack harmful T cells without triggering the same problem of engineered T cells killing each other.

"NK cells can treat these T cell malignancies -- not only T cell cancer, but also T cell autoimmune diseases," Chen says.

Producing CAR NK cells outside the body, however, still requires much of the specialized equipment, labor, and processing associated with CAR T cell manufacturing. To overcome these limitations, the MIT team investigated whether NK cells could instead be engineered "in vivo," meaning directly inside the body.

"If a patient can just get an infusion of nanoparticles, it would dramatically simplify the process and reduce costs," Anderson says.

Although researchers are actively developing CAR NK cell therapies for cancer and autoimmune disorders, none have received FDA approval.

How mRNA Nanoparticles Reprogram Immune Cells

The MIT team designed lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) capable of transporting messenger RNA into natural killer cells. The mRNA carries instructions for producing a chimeric antigen receptor that directs the modified immune cell toward a specific target.

The technology can be adapted to recognize different proteins depending on the disease being treated. For example, the researchers can provide instructions for a receptor that recognizes CD19, a protein found on B cells, or CD3, a protein present on T cells, including those responsible for autoimmune attacks.

To help the nanoparticles reach the correct immune cells, the scientists covered their surfaces with antibody fragments. These fragments recognize and attach to receptors on NK cells, helping deliver the genetic instructions where they are needed.

Once inside an NK cell, the mRNA directs the production of the new receptor, giving the immune cell the ability to recognize and attack its intended target.

The researchers then tested whether this approach could efficiently reprogram NK cells and whether the resulting cells could combat cancer and autoimmune disease in mice.

Reprogrammed Immune Cells Eliminate Tumors in Mice

The initial experiments produced encouraging results. After injecting the nanoparticles into mice, the researchers successfully modified approximately 80 percent of the NK cells they were targeting.

They next investigated whether these engineered cells could attack tumors. In mice with an aggressive form of melanoma, three of the five animals treated with nanoparticles designed to direct NK cells against the cancer experienced complete remission.

The researchers also tested the technique against T cell lymphoma using humanized mice. These animals receive transfusions of human blood cells, temporarily giving them immune systems that share certain characteristics with those of humans.

In this model, the treatment produced substantial tumor destruction. After five injections of the nanoparticles, the tumors were completely eliminated.

Importantly, these results were comparable to those achieved with CAR NK cells produced through the more traditional method of collecting NK cells, modifying them outside the body, and then returning them to the animals.

This suggests that generating CAR NK cells directly inside the body could offer similar cancer-fighting capabilities while avoiding the complicated manufacturing process required by conventional cell therapies.

A Single Injection Reverses Autoimmune Liver Damage

The researchers also wanted to determine whether their technology could help treat autoimmune diseases, in which the immune system mistakenly damages healthy tissues.

They focused on autoimmune hepatitis, a condition in which abnormal T cells attack hepatocytes, the main functional cells of the liver. By designing nanoparticles that instruct NK cells to recognize these harmful T cells, the scientists tested whether they could interrupt the autoimmune response.

The treatment successfully eliminated the autoreactive T cells in mice with the disease. Even more encouragingly, the animals' damaged liver tissue healed after the harmful immune cells were removed.

These improvements occurred after just one nanoparticle injection, demonstrating the potential of the approach beyond cancer treatment.

"This study is an excellent example of the power of nano delivery systems and their ability to potentially treat cancer and other diseases," Langer says.

A New Direction for Cancer and Autoimmune Treatments

The researchers believe that reprogramming natural killer cells inside the body could eventually provide new treatment options for a much wider range of conditions.

Among the diseases they hope to target are multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis, both of which can involve harmful immune responses driven by dysfunctional T cells.

Although the findings are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice, and further research will be necessary to determine whether the technique is safe and effective in humans.

If successful, the technology could make engineered immune cell treatments considerably more accessible by replacing a lengthy laboratory manufacturing process with the direct delivery of genetic instructions through nanoparticles.

The research received funding from Sanofi, the Marble Center for Cancer Nanomedicine, and a Koch Institute Support (core) Grant from the National Cancer Institute.

#5666. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed on restoring trust in science, the state of public health, and RFK Jr.

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Nicholas Florko covers trust in science for STAT, aiming to help readers understand the lived experiences of people who distrust science and to probe why that distrust exists and its consequences. Reach him on Signal at nickflorko.44

Abdul El-Sayed will soon become the first epidemiologist in the Senate at a moment that would keep anyone with a public health background up at night. More than 5,000 Americans have been sickened by the measles this year and the United States is expected to lose its formal measles elimination status by the end of the month. Dengue fever is spreading in Florida, respiratory virus season is underway, and the United States just weathered a foodborne illness outbreak that sickened more than 20,000.

In a wide-ranging interview with STAT, the Michigan Democrat emphasized that he is hopeful the United States can fix its growing trust-in-science problem, but he expressed frustration — at Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., at drug and insurance companies, and at the field of public health — for leading America down this path.

Below, El-Sayed speaks about his plan to rebuild trust in science and public health, his intentions toward Kennedy, and how gatekeeping has kept scientific discoveries from the public. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.

“We’ve created the space for a few grifters to come in and in effect lie to the public,” El-Sayed said. “To create a level of distrust in science and in public health that has had disastrous consequences.”

As the senator-elect from Michigan, how can you help restore trust in health and science? What can you do from Washington to improve these issues?

Well, No. 1, I think you can start taking on greed. Which is why I support “Medicare for All,” because it gets the greed of the insurance industry and the greed of the pharmaceutical industry and the greed of the hospital corporations out of the way so folks can benefit from the incredible things that science creates.

No. 2, I think you have to show the grifters for who they are and how they are, the ways that they use big words that they don’t understand to trick the public, the ways that there’s always a catch at the end where they’re making money off of their grift.

And No. 3, I want to reinvigorate a movement for public health that is willing to stand up to the power of big corporations. … I think we need to be willing to pick a righteous fight in service of the public health.

You’ve mentioned your eagerness to investigate RFK Jr. Are you concerned at all that grilling RFK could serve to further polarize the people that do believe in him?

You can grill a steak and get it to perfect medium rare, or you can grill a steak and it’s well done and inedible, the way the president likes it.

The mistake would be to focus on areas that are polarizing. I wanna understand why he DOGE’d away or he allowed the DOGE’ing away of the CDC [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] and the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] in ways that left us eating crap lettuce. I want to understand why he hasn’t led the effort to take on the pesticides that are in our food or the additives in our food, why he’s kowtowing to the same corporations he said he was going to stand up to. I want to understand that. Let’s start there.

I’m curious if you have a message to the people that do support Kennedy on why they should trust someone like you on issues of public health.

Well, he told you he’s gonna stand up to the corporations. He hasn’t. I have.

There’s no candidate who’s taken more spending against them in a primary election in their own party than I have, not in history. So at least you know I’m gonna stand up.

I’ve spent my whole career trying to make people healthier, trying to address the greed in our health care system.

There’s all this talk of back and forth: Should RFK Jr. be investigated? Should he be removed? What’s your latest thinking on this?

I think we focus too much on him. I think the bigger question is how do we build the CDC and FDA and NIH [National Institutes of Health] that are worthy of the people that they serve, and that’s gonna always be my focus.

So any investigation that we’re doing is about trying to correct the problems and address the flaws and the faults rather than trying to achieve any sort of retribution.

The people are struggling. They are suffering. They can barely afford groceries, can barely afford gas, can barely see a doctor, are worried about the air they’re breathing, the water they’re drinking, the quality of groceries they’re even buying for an exorbitant price.

My job is to serve them. The personalities involved are secondary to me. My job is to go in and figure out what went wrong, how do we fix it, and how do we hold accountable the people who — if they knowingly broke something — how we do we hold them accountable for it. It’s that simple. It’s less about the personalities. I think we focus too much on that.

There’s been this desire among folks within your party to find common ground with RFK on issues. Are there issues that you think you could work with RFK and his team on, or are we kind of past that?

If he actually wants to show up and start doing the things he said he was going to do on pollutants, on additives, sure. I’ll work with anyone. He could be wrong on 95 things, but if he’s right on five, I’ll work with him on those five and hold him accountable for the 95.

Obviously Democrats can’t fix all of these issues. Trust issues started before RFK and I’m sure they’ll go on past RFK. How do you think about how we should judge Democrats’ progress on these issues?

Are we achieving goals that keep people healthy, reduce their costs, empower them. … If we’re doing that, then we’re winning and we’re succeeding. If not, then we’re not. I want people to be able to be their healthiest and their wealthiest. That’s really the bottom line.

It seems like a foregone conclusion, the U.S. will lose its measles elimination status.  Do you have thoughts on that?

It’s a travesty. We didn’t have to get here. In a lot of ways, obviously, I blame mis- and dis-information mongers like RFK Jr. for that, but I also blame our collective scientific and health care apparatus for creating the circumstances where somebody like him could step in, and he would have a willing audience willing to listen.

Where did we go wrong in making health care so untrustworthy that somebody with such limited cognitive ability and who is so obviously a grifter, where he could step in and change so many minds? That’s on us.

The belief that the measles vaccine causes autism is going up over time, and it’s been debunked for 20 years. … How do we break through here?

It starts with basic science education. … Too often the way that scientists speak is about speaking to other scientists to make themselves sound smarter rather than speaking to the public, to help the public feel as smart as they really are. By making sure that everybody understands how and why these things work. Science for the public good … that ethos is something that we’ve forgotten. And I really, desperately want us to remember it.

Science is a gift. It’s a beautiful, incredible gift, and we missed the opportunity to communicate it in all of its elegance because too often it is this thing that is sort of held among the scientific community for consumption by the scientific community. And then we allow a lot of our best science to sit behind paywalls people can’t hop over. So there’s a resentment that happens in publicly funded science for the most part, and we’re keeping [it] out of the hands of people who need it most.

These are big structural questions that ought to animate the way we do science for the rest of the 21st century, and I’m hoping that I can use my role as a doctor and a scientist in the Senate to start driving that conversation among the folks in science.

You can focus on RFK Jr. all you want, but he identified a set of weaknesses that those of us who have committed our lives to science and the public’s health that we allowed to exist in the first place.

How hopeful are you that we can solve these trust issues?

I wouldn’t be doing this if I didn’t believe we could. Science always wins.  I just hope that it wins quickly. But the beautiful thing about science is that in the end it always finds the right answer.

#5665. Mastering Digital Marketing - How to Grow Your Business Online

Having a solid digital marketing strategy is essential if you want to succeed as a business owner in the modern day. Effective digital marketing lets you get more eyes on your business and ensure consistent growth.

Because digital marketing trends are forever changing, it’s important to stay on top of your brand’s strategy. Doing so ensures that you stand out above your competitors and gain the recognition that your brand deserves.

If you’re unsure how to master your digital marketing strategy, consider working with an expert company that can help you figure out which direction to go. A professional agency, such as Scorpion Digital Marketing Agency, can support your online efforts to maximize your success.

If you don’t want to outsource your digital marketing processes, try these top tips below to maintain an effective digital marketing strategy and boost your business growth.

Your website is where most of your new audience will find your business and your existing customers will shop for your new products and services. If you create a strong first impression through your website, you can gain credibility and authority in your industry.

Make sure to regularly update your website content so it’s accurate and on-trend. Doing so also signals to Google that your website is authoritative and credible, increasing your rankings on search engine results pages (SERPs).

The higher your rankings, the higher your visibility, meaning you can expand your reach with minimal effort. When updating your content, use plenty of industry-relevant keywords and key phrases to ensure your target audience finds your site.

With a strong social media strategy, you can significantly expand your reach and gain recognition as a trustworthy brand. Regularly posting content enables you to provide consistent value to your audience while displaying your expertise.

You can create posts highlighting the benefits of your products or the quality of your services. You can share positive testimonials and reviews from happy customers to build your credibility.

Social media platforms allow you to connect directly with your target audience too. You can answer queries and concerns in your DMs and show the human side of your brand.

Video marketing is becoming increasingly effective. Over four-fifths of consumer internet traffic comes from videos, so it's the perfect way to expand your reach and drive more traffic to your website.

Whether you use live or pre-filmed video content, you can capture your target audience's attention and provide helpful information in an engaging way. You can share demonstrations of how to use your products or explain your services in more detail to persuade consumers to check out your brand.

Optimize your videos for search engines by including keywords and phrases in your video titles and descriptions. Doing so increases your rankings on SERPs and puts your brand in front of as many people as possible.

#5664. EXCLUSIVE: Olympic Champion Tara Lipinski Shares Her ‘Controversial’ Christmas Decorating Rule—and Why She’s Starting Now

Olympic figure skating champion Tara Lipinski is picking sides in some of the most divisive holiday decor debates of all time as she hosts HGTV’s "Big Bargain Holiday Showdown."

The 44-year-old Lipinski, who earned gold in the 1998 Winter Games, reveals her holiday decor rules to Realtor.com® ahead of the Nov. 10 premiere of the new six-episode competition series.

She covers everything from when it's appropriate to start decorating to when decorations should be removed, and whether Christmas lights are better in multicolor or monotone.

On the show, two teams of family, friends, and neighbors go head-to-head in a holiday-themed design battle where they have just 48 hours and $500 to overhaul one room in their respective homes.

DIY experts Ashley Dixon and Clinton Tharp are on hand to help wrap things up before designers Stephen Brown and Pelar Fullilove judge the spaces and declare the winner of a $2,000 cash prize.

"I know it's very controversial, but I am starting to decorate this week. I am skipping Thanksgiving," Lipinski, who stays in her lane as a neutral host on the HGTV show, tells Realtor.com.

"The older I get, the wider the window has become. I really don't think it can be too early. It's just so fun to walk into your house when it's full of Christmas lights and so cozy and idyllic and warm. ... I like to stretch it as much as I can. That’s why in November, you have a ton of time, you can just relish in it."

Lipinski clarifies that, although she'll set her table to host Thanksgiving, it's jingle all the way until the start of the New Year.

"I always used to take it down right away. I do get a little tired of it when holidays are actually over, so I feel like you've got, like, one week after and then you've got to zip it up," she says.

In Lipinski’s house, which she shares with husband Todd Kapostasy and their 3-year-old daughter, Georgie, the holiday magic is spread in multiple spaces.

"We usually go [for] a more traditional Christmas, the classic, the red, the green," she shares. "Other rooms, we change it up. We do our bedroom a whole winter wonderland, white and gold and silver. And then Georgie, my daughter's room, we do a really fun pink Christmas so we can branch out.

"I feel like it's evolved throughout the years, and there's always adding and subtracting."

There is only one thing that never changes: the Christmas tree.

“We have a lot of artificial trees in the house, but for the one in the living room, our main one, we do a real one,” says Lipinski. “My husband loves that, so that's been his thing since we got married. We've always done a real tree. It's fun. That day we make it a tradition and get dressed up in our Christmas outfit and we go and pick out a tree and make it festive.”

The decision to go faux with trees everywhere except the living room has always been unanimous, but the couple have clashed in the past.

“My husband and I have gotten into a full-blown argument about the amount of Christmas lights that need to be on a tree. He fully understands now that it has to be every inch covered,” she says.

As for whether the Christmas tree lights should be a string of assorted colors or all white, Lipinski says for her house, it depends on the tree’s location.

“I like it to be the multicolored ones. That’s my go-to. Although the ones in my bedroom, since it's all the white theme, we do just the white,” she details.

Lipinski has been honing her holiday home design technique for decades. She credits her mother for inspiring a passion for all the pageantry.

“My mom was meant to be an interior designer, so I grew up with someone who was constantly making our house a home and making it so special, that loves decorating, and I have that same gene,” she shares.

“We are big holiday people. We have a storage unit of not just Christmas [decor]. We decorate every single holiday, so this show just feels like it was meant for both of us. After all the things I've done in my career, I feel like she's probably going to be most proud of this one because it's so spot-on.”

The annual task of decorating the home has become a festive event for the whole family.

“What's fun is my mom and dad still come over, and they decorate with me,” says Lipinski. “My dad's the handy one and my mom is so creative. I couldn't do it without them. We pull out the boxes, we put on Christmas music, we have some hot cocoa, and we decorate together. It's really become a tradition, and now [with] my daughter, it feels like the three generations all together doing it still.”

The family’s dedication to holiday decor already seems to be something Lipinski’s daughter is developing herself.

“The art of decorating, making it special, and doing it with family is what I'm passing down to my daughter—and that we do it together. She loves it,” shares Lipinski. “This year, she's finally really clocking what Christmas is. When I told her it's time to decorate, her eyes lit up, and I just thought, 'Oh, my goodness, I'm creating a little monster here.’”

This year, Lipinski and her team of holiday fanatics plan to spruce up their space with even more trimmings thanks to the seasonal inspiration the show’s creative contestants have gifted.

“Really opening your mind ... the way they utilize the space of the room, like using the chandelier, there [were] some really beautiful entries," she says.

"It felt super immersive and even more magical, so I'm going to try to up the ante this year on my own Christmas decorating from learning those things.”

'Big Bargain Holiday Showdown' premieres on Nov. 10 at 9 p.m. on HGTV and streams the next day on HBO Max.

Karli Mullane is a celebrity and entertainment journalist at Realtor.com. She previously worked at Celeb Map, POPSUGAR, and NBC, covering pop culture, lifestyle, travel, and news of all kinds. Karli earned a BA in History from UCLA and an MA in Broadcast Journalism from San Francisco State University. She is equally grateful to have reported from both Hollywood red carpets and the comfort of her Bay Area home.
